pages.title: 9. Worked example – FIFO in a rising market (Nairobi retailer)
pages.markdown:
## 9. Worked example – FIFO in a rising market (Nairobi retailer)

**Kamau Electronics** sells phone chargers:

| Date | Units | Cost (Sh.) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Jun stock | 100 | 500 |
| 10 Jun purchase | 200 | 550 |
| 18 Jun sale | 250 | – |
| 25 Jun purchase | 150 | 600 |

**FIFO:** 18 Jun sale of 250 = 100 × 500 + 150 × 550 → COGS 132,500. Left: 50 × 550 = 27,500; plus 25 Jun 150 × 600 = 90,000. **Closing stock = Sh. 117,500.** Check: goods available = 50,000 + 110,000 + 90,000 = 250,000 = COGS 132,500 + closing 117,500 ✓.

**AVCO (periodic):** 250,000 ÷ 450 = 555.56; COGS = 250 × 555.56 = 138,889; closing = 200 × 555.56 = 111,111 ✓.

Notice FIFO profit is higher (lower COGS) when prices rise — the standard exam conclusion, and the reason IAS 2 bans LIFO.

pages.title: 10. Common exam traps
pages.markdown:
## 10. Common exam traps

1. **LIFO is prohibited** by IAS 2 — never use it in answers, even if the question "invites" a comparison.
2. FIFO vs AVCO: in **rising prices**, FIFO → higher closing stock and higher profit; in falling prices the reverse.
3. Provision: first year = full amount; later years = **movement only**; decreases are credited to P&L (income).
4. Bad debt write-off vs provision: write-off removes the debtor; provision is an estimate against debtors still carried.
5. Control accounts: **debits in personal accounts → debits in control** (same side). Sales are debited to the sales control; cash received is credited.
6. NRV write-down hits **P&L immediately**; reversals reduce expense.
7. The sales ledger control's **credit balances c/d** (customers who overpaid) appear on the *debit* side as balances carried down — list them on the correct side or the control will not balance.
8. In FIFO questions, always prove **goods available for sale = COGS + closing stock** before moving on — it catches the arithmetic slips that cost the most marks.

1. **LIFO is prohibited** by IAS 2 — never use it in answers.
2. FIFO vs AVCO: in **rising prices**, FIFO → higher closing stock and higher profit.
3. Provision: first year = full amount; later years = **movement only**; decreases are credited to P&L.
4. Bad debt write-off vs provision: write-off removes the debtor; provision is an estimate against debtors still carried.
5. Control accounts: **debits in personal accounts → debits in control** (same side). Sales are debited to the sales control; cash received is credited.
6. NRV write-down hits **P&L immediately**; reversals reduce expense.

pages.title: Key terms (flashcards)
pages.markdown:
## Key terms (flashcards)

- **IAS 2** – Inventories: lower of cost and NRV; FIFO or weighted average.
- **Net realizable value (NRV)** – Estimated selling price less costs of completion and sale.
- **FIFO** – First-in, first-out: oldest costs to COGS; newest costs in closing stock.
- **Weighted average (AVCO)** – Average cost of all units available for sale.
- **Carriage inwards** – Transport costs bringing inventory to location/condition; part of cost.
- **Trade receivables** – Amounts due from credit customers; current assets.
- **Bad debt** – Irrecoverable amount written off: Dr Bad debts / Cr Debtor, then to P&L.
- **Provision for doubtful debts** – Estimate of amounts that may not be collected; specific or general.
- **Control account** – General-ledger total account mirroring a subsidiary ledger (sales/purchases).
- **Contra / set-off** – Offsetting a balance that is both debtor and creditor.

pages.title: Module summary
pages.markdown:
## Module summary

IAS 2 measures inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value, using FIFO or weighted average (never LIFO). Cost includes purchase, conversion and carriage inwards; write-downs hit profit or loss immediately. Trade receivables are carried less bad debts written off (Dr Bad debts / Cr Debtor, then to P&L) and provisions for doubtful debts — full provision in year one, movements only thereafter. Sales and purchases ledger control accounts mirror the subsidiary ledgers and must agree with them.

pages.title: Exam day tips
pages.markdown:
## Exam day tips

- Inventory computations: prove goods available = COGS + closing stock — catches arithmetic slips.
- Provision questions: build the three-column table (debtors, %, required) then compute movements.
- Control accounts: list every item from the question, tick it off as posted, then balance.

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# Cash, Bank and Reconciliations

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

1. Explain why the cash book and bank statement balances differ.
2. Identify the causes of difference: unpresented cheques, uncredited deposits, bank charges, direct debits/credits, standing orders, dishonoured cheques, interest, errors.
3. Prepare an **updated (adjusted) cash book**.
4. Prepare a **bank reconciliation statement** in both formats (from cash book; from bank statement).
5. Handle overdraft situations in reconciliations.

---

pages.title: 1. Why reconcile?
pages.markdown:
## 1. Why reconcile?

The cash book (bank columns) records the firm's view; the **bank statement** records the bank's view. Ideally identical — in practice almost never. The **bank reconciliation statement** identifies every difference (**reconciling items**) so that the **adjusted cash book balance and adjusted bank statement balance agree**. Functions: update the cash book (bank charges, direct debits); check/correct cash book errors; detect and prevent fraud.

pages.title: 2. Causes of difference
pages.markdown:
## 2. Causes of difference

**Timing differences (no cash book update needed):**
- **Unpresented cheques** – issued and recorded, not yet presented → bank balance *higher* than cash book.
- **Uncredited deposits (deposits in transit)** – banked and recorded, not yet credited by the bank → bank balance *lower*.

**Items the firm learns from the statement (update the cash book first):**
- **Bank charges** and overdraft interest – Dr Bank charges / Cr Cash book (bank).
- **Standing orders / direct debits** (loan repayments, utilities) – Dr Expense/Liability / Cr Cash book.
- **Direct credits** (dividends, customer direct deposits, notes collected) – Dr Cash book / Cr Income/Debtor.
- **Interest earned** – Dr Cash book / Cr Interest income.
- **Dishonoured (NSF) cheques** – a deposited cheque bounces: Dr Debtor / Cr Cash book (write it back).
- **Errors in the cash book** – over/undercasts, transpositions, mispostings: correct via journal to cash book.

**Bank errors** – adjusted on the *bank statement* side of the reconciliation (and reported to the bank), never in the cash book.

**Golden procedure:** (1) update the cash book for all items it should have recorded; (2) reconcile the *updated* balance to the bank statement using unpresented cheques and uncredited deposits (± bank errors).

![Bank reconciliation](https://jorjhskqykkajcaiweqn.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/course-media/ca11/m03-accounting-for-assets-and-liabilities/illustrations/bank-reconciliation.png)

pages.title: 3. The two formats
pages.markdown:
## 3. The two formats

**Format 1 (start from updated cash book):**
```
Balance as per cash book (updated)                        xxx
Add: unpresented cheques                            xxx
     bank-statement errors increasing balance       xxx   xxx
                                                          xxx
Less: uncredited deposits                           xxx
      bank-statement errors decreasing balance      xxx  (xxx)
Balance as per bank statement                             xxx
```

**Format 2 (start from bank statement):**
```
Balance as per bank statement                             xxx
Add: uncredited deposits                            xxx
     bank errors (decreasing type)                  xxx   xxx
                                                          xxx
Less: unpresented cheques                           xxx
      bank errors (increasing type)                 xxx  (xxx)
Balance as per cash book (updated)                        xxx
```

Logic check: unpresented cheques make the bank balance too *high* → subtract from bank side / add to cash-book side. Uncredited deposits make it too *low* → add to bank side / subtract from cash-book side.

pages.title: 4. Worked example 1 – Joseph Kahiga, December 2005 (from the book, Sh.)
pages.markdown:
## 4. Worked example 1 – Joseph Kahiga, December 2005 (from the book, Sh.)

Cash book balance 31 Dec: **179,300**; bank statement balance: **155,700**.

**Step 1 – update the cash book** (items on the statement not in the cash book): dividend received 2,600 (Dr Cash book / Cr Dividend income); standing order 3,200; bank charges 1,800; direct debit 8,800 (all Cr Cash book).

```
Updated cash book: 179,300 + 2,600 − 3,200 − 1,800 − 8,800 = Sh. 168,100
```

(Cheques 417869 Victor Karanja 7,100 and 417872 Steve Maithya 3,700 were in the cash book but not on the statement → unpresented. Deposits by Owen Ndumbi 9,800 and Walter Oyugi 13,400 were in the cash book but not credited → uncredited.)

**Step 2 – reconciliation (Format 1):**

| | Sh. | Sh. |
|---|---|---|
| Balance as per cash book (updated) | | 168,100 |
| Add: unpresented cheques (7,100 + 3,700) | | 10,800 |
| | | 178,900 |
| Less: uncredited deposits (9,800 + 13,400) | | (23,200) |
| **Balance as per bank statement** | | **155,700** ✓ |

pages.title: 5. Worked example 2 – Mwambi, June 2001 (from the book, Sh.)
pages.markdown:
## 5. Worked example 2 – Mwambi, June 2001 (from the book, Sh.)

Cash book 2,366,500; bank statement 706,500. Investigation:

**Cash book updates:** bank charges 3,000 (Cr); unrecorded receipts 26,500 (Dr); standing order 62,000 (Cr); payment entered as 79,400 instead of 74,900 → overcast 4,500 (Dr); dishonoured cheque 15,000 (Cr); opening balance brought forward as debit 329,250 instead of credit → correct by 2 × 329,250 = **658,500** (Cr); old cheque written back but already honoured 44,000 (Cr); customer deposits of 832,500 credited by the bank to the *wrong account* — already entered in Mwambi's cash book on customers' word → this is a **bank error**, not a cash book item (no entry).

```
Adjusted cash book: 2,366,500 + 26,500 + 4,500 − 3,000 − 62,000 − 658,500 − 15,000 − 44,000 = Sh. 1,615,000
```

**Reconciliation:** 1,615,000 + unpresented cheques 22,500 − uncredited deposits 98,500 − bank error 832,500 = **706,500** ✓.

**Exam traps on display:** the 658,500 double-correction for a wrong-side brought-forward balance; the 832,500 wrong-account credit is a *bank* error (reconciliation side only); and the 44,000 written-back cheque that was already honoured — a reminder that "reversing" entries in the cash book must always be checked against what the bank actually did.

pages.title: 6. Quick-fire practice (self-test)
pages.markdown:
## 6. Quick-fire practice (self-test)

1. Cash book Dr 48,000; bank statement Cr 51,500; unpresented cheques 12,000; uncredited deposits 8,000; bank charges 500 not in cash book. → Updated cash book: 48,000 − 500 = 47,500; reconciliation: 47,500 + 12,000 − 8,000 = **51,500** ✓. The discipline: **always prove the final line** equals the given balance.
2. A customer pays Sh. 20,000 directly into the bank; you find it on the statement. → Dr Cash book 20,000 / Cr Debtor 20,000 (cash book update — it never appears in the reconciliation).
3. A cheque you issued for Sh. 15,000 is still unpresented after 6 months. → It stays an unpresented cheque until it is presented or becomes stale and is written back (Dr Cash book / Cr Creditor).

pages.title: 6. Overdrafts in reconciliations
pages.markdown:
## 6. Overdrafts in reconciliations

An **overdraft** = withdrawals beyond zero balance (prior agreement = agreed rate; beyond = fees/higher rates). In the cash book it is a **credit balance**; on the bank statement it appears as a **debit** balance (to the bank, the customer's account is a liability). The book's Lotus Ltd illustration runs two accounts with mixed Dr/Cr balances — apply the same two-step procedure per account, keeping the signs straight: e.g. Account 1: cash book (25,600) Cr + unpresented/transfer adjustments 429,200 − uncredited 80,000 = bank statement 323,600 Cr ✓.

pages.title: 7. Worked example 3 – the two-account overdraft case (book: Lotus Ltd, March 2004, Sh.)
pages.markdown:
## 7. Worked example 3 – the two-account overdraft case (book: Lotus Ltd, March 2004, Sh.)

Lotus Ltd operates two bank accounts. Balances: Account 1 — bank statement 323,600 (Cr), cash book 34,000 (Dr); Account 2 — bank statement 156,400 (Dr), cash book 277,600 (Dr).

**Updated cash book No. 1 (book's figures):** Dr: balance b/d 34,000; direct credit (cheque M420) 8,800; cheque B308 (wrongly entered in account 1) 12,800; balance c/d 25,600 → 81,200. Cr: bank charges 1,200; cheque D720 wrongly entered in account 1 (belongs to account 2) 80,000 → 81,200 ✓.

**Reconciliation No. 1 (book's figures):** Balance as per adjusted cash book (25,600); Add: cheque A210 bank error 29,200 + unexecuted transfer 400,000 = 429,200 → 403,600; Less: uncredited cheques 80,000 → **323,600** = bank statement ✓. (The 400,000 transfer was entered in the cash book but the bank was never instructed — a classic "bank-side" timing/error item.)

**Updated cash book No. 2:** Dr: balance b/d 277,600; direct cheque D720 80,000; cheque H785 understated 400 → 358,000. Cr: dishonoured cheque F301 8,000; cheque K341 overstated 1,600; cheque B308 12,800; standing order 4,000; cheque BJ48 understated 3,600; bank charges 1,600; balance c/d 326,400 → 358,000 ✓.

**Sign rule to memorise:** in the cash book an overdraft is a **credit** balance (a liability of the business); on the bank statement it is a **debit** balance (the customer's account is a liability *of the bank*). Keep the minus sign on the overdrawn side through every line — most errors come from dropping it halfway.

pages.title: 8. Common exam traps
pages.markdown:
## 8. Common exam traps

1. **Update the cash book FIRST** — then reconcile. Doing it in one step muddles timing vs error items.
2. Unpresented cheques vs uncredited deposits: say out loud which side each pushes.
3. Dishonoured cheques go back to the **debtor** (Dr Debtor / Cr Cash book) — never to sales.
4. Bank errors are **never** adjusted in the cash book.
5. A wrong-side brought-forward balance needs a **double** correction.
6. Direct debits/standing orders/dividends discovered on the statement → cash book update, then they vanish from the reconciliation.

pages.title: Key terms (flashcards)
pages.markdown:
## Key terms (flashcards)

- **Bank reconciliation statement** – Statement explaining the difference between the cash book and bank statement balances.
- **Unpresented cheques** – Issued and recorded but not yet presented; bank balance overstated.
- **Uncredited deposits (deposits in transit)** – Banked and recorded but not yet credited; bank balance understated.
- **Bank charges** – Service fees; updated in the cash book (Dr Bank charges).
- **Standing order / direct debit** – Automatic payments; updated in the cash book when first seen on the statement.
- **Dishonoured (NSF) cheque** – Bounced deposited cheque; written back: Dr Debtor / Cr Cash book.
- **Updated/adjusted cash book** – Cash book corrected for bank-originated items and errors before reconciling.
- **Bank overdraft** – Negative bank balance; credit balance in the cash book, debit balance on the statement.
- **Credit/debit memoranda** – Bank notices of automatic deposits (credit memo) and withdrawals (debit memo).

pages.title: Module summary
pages.markdown:
## Module summary

The bank reconciliation explains the difference between the cash book and the bank statement. First update the cash book for bank-originated items (charges, standing orders, direct debits/credits, interest, dishonoured cheques, dividends) and cash book errors; then reconcile the updated balance to the statement using timing differences — unpresented cheques and uncredited deposits (plus any bank errors). Bank errors are never adjusted in the cash book, and overdrafts simply reverse the signs.

pages.title: Exam day tips
pages.markdown:
## Exam day tips

- Rule two workings: "Updated cash book" then "Bank reconciliation statement" — label every line.
- Tick each statement item against the cash book as you go; un-ticked items drive both workings.
- Prove the final line equals the given statement/cash book balance — the examiner checks it.

chapters.lesson: Liabilities — Payables, Loans, Accruals and Prepayments

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# Liabilities — Payables, Loans, Accruals and Prepayments

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

1. Define liabilities and classify them (current vs non-current).
2. Explain bank overdrafts and their causes.
3. Maintain trade payables control accounts, including contras and bills of exchange.
4. Account for loan receipt, interest accrual and repayment (principal vs interest).
5. Account for accrued expenses, prepaid expenses, accrued income and prepaid (unearned) income with ledger entries.
6. Show accruals/prepayments in the income statement and statement of financial position.

---

pages.title: 1. Nature and classification of liabilities
pages.markdown:
## 1. Nature and classification of liabilities

A **liability** is a present obligation arising from past events, to be settled by an outflow of resources. **Trade payables** (accounts payable) = money owed to creditors/suppliers for goods or services; **short-term** if due within 12 months, **long-term** beyond. Other liabilities: bank overdrafts, loans, accruals, prepaid income.

pages.title: 2. Bank overdraft
pages.markdown:
## 2. Bank overdraft

An overdraft occurs when withdrawals drive the available balance **below zero** ("overdrawn"). With a prior agreement and within the limit, interest runs at the agreed rate; beyond the terms, extra fees and higher rates apply. The book lists causes: intentional short-term borrowing; failure to keep an accurate account register; ATM overdrafts; temporary deposit holds; unexpected electronic withdrawals; authorization holds on debit cards; unexpected bank fees; "playing the float"; returned (bounced) cheque deposits; fraud; bank errors; victimization (identity theft); intraday overdrafts. In the books an overdraft is a **credit balance** in the cash book and a **current liability** in the statement of financial position.

pages.title: 3. Trade payables control accounts
pages.markdown:
## 3. Trade payables control accounts

Same principles as Lesson 4's receivables control (mirror image). The **purchases ledger control** balance (credit) must equal total creditors. Format (Sh.):

| Dr | Sh. | Cr | Sh. |
|---|---|---|---|
| Debit balances b/d | xxx | Credit balances b/d | xxx |
| Cash/cheques paid to creditors | xxx | Credit purchases (purchases journal) | xxx |
| Discounts received | xxx | Refunds from suppliers | xxx |
| Allowances by suppliers | xxx | Debit balances c/d | xxx |
| Sales ledger contras | xxx | | |
| Returns outwards | xxx | | |
| Credit balances c/d | xxx | | |

**Bills of exchange:** bills payable (accepted) reduce the creditor: Dr Creditor / Cr Bills payable; on dishonour: Dr Bills payable / Cr Creditor (plus charges). The book's XML Ltd trade payables control (Dec 2014) balances at **Sh. 10,406,500** with closing credit balance **Sh. 4,355,000** (see Lesson 4 for the full working).

pages.title: 4. Loans – principal vs interest
pages.markdown:
## 4. Loans – principal vs interest

A loan = debt evidenced by a note stating **principal**, **interest rate** and **repayment date**. Repayment is typically by instalments. **Accounting rule:** never report loan receipt as revenue or repayment as expense — both are **statement of financial position** movements: receipt Dr Cash / Cr Loan (liability); repayment Dr Loan / Cr Cash; interest Dr Interest expense (P&L) / Cr Cash (or accrued interest payable if unpaid at year-end).

### Worked example

Biashara Ltd borrows Sh. 1,200,000 on 1 Jul 2025, 12% p.a., repayable in 12 equal monthly instalments of principal (Sh. 100,000) plus interest on the reducing balance. Year-end 31 Dec 2025 (6 instalments paid):

| Month | Principal repaid | Interest (12%/12 × balance) |
|---|---|---|
| Jul | 100,000 | 12,000 |
| Aug | 100,000 | 11,000 |
| Sep | 100,000 | 10,000 |
| Oct | 100,000 | 9,000 |
| Nov | 100,000 | 8,000 |
| Dec | 100,000 | 7,000 |
| **Total** | **600,000** | **57,000** |

Entries at year-end: Dr Loan 600,000 / Cr Bank 600,000 (principal); Dr Interest expense 57,000 / Cr Bank 57,000. Statement of financial position: loan liability **Sh. 600,000** (current — repayable within 12 months of year-end); P&L: interest **Sh. 57,000**. **Exam trap:** only the interest hits profit or loss — the principal never does.

pages.title: 5. Accruals and prepayments
pages.markdown:
## 5. Accruals and prepayments

![Accruals and prepayments 2x2 grid](https://jorjhskqykkajcaiweqn.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/course-media/ca11/m03-accounting-for-assets-and-liabilities/illustrations/accruals-grid.png)

The **accruals concept**: recognise income/expenses in the period to which they relate.

### Accrued expenses (owed at year-end → current liability)
Dr Expense (P&L, full period cost) / Cr Accrual (SOFP). Example: electricity for December Sh. 36,710 invoiced in January: Dr Electricity 36,710 / Cr Accruals 36,710.

### Prepaid expenses (paid in advance → current asset)
Dr Prepayment (SOFP) / Cr Expense. Book example: insurance Sh. 10,000 paid 1 Apr for 12 months, year-end 31 Dec → 3/12 prepaid = **Sh. 2,500**: P&L charge 7,500; SOFP prepayment 2,500.

### Accrued income (earned, not received → current asset)
Dr Accrued income receivable (SOFP) / Cr Income (P&L). Book example: rent Sh. 2,000/month received in arrears; at 31 Dec, December's Sh. 2,000 accrued: P&L rent income 24,000 (full year), SOFP accrued rent **2,000**.

### Prepaid (unearned) income (received in advance → current liability)
Dr Income (P&L, defer) / Cr Prepaid income (SOFP). Book example: rent Sh. 5,000/month, quarterly in advance from 1 Mar; 4 × 15,000 = 60,000 received; 2 months (Jan–Feb) unearned = **Sh. 10,000**: P&L rent income 50,000; SOFP prepaid rent **10,000** (liability).

### Comprehensive worked example (book: Fwamba Enterprises, 31 Dec 2004, Sh. '000)

- **Insurance:** paid 32,000; policy 15,000 paid 1 Jul 2004 covers to 30 Jun 2005 → prepaid 6/12 × 15,000 = **7,500**. P&L 24,500; SOFP prepayment 7,500.
- **Commission:** received 10,000; earned but not received 5,000 → accrued income. P&L 15,000; SOFP accrued income 5,000.
- **Rent and rates:** opening — rent owing 13,000 (accrual b/d), rates prepaid 4,500; paid during year 65,000; closing — rent owing 16,000, rates prepaid 2,500. P&L charge = 65,000 + 13,000... let's prove: Rent and rates account: Dr side: balance b/d (prepaid rates) 4,500 + bank 65,000 + balance c/d (accrued rent) 16,000 = 85,500; Cr side: balance b/d (accrued rent) 13,000 + P&L (bal. fig.) 70,000 + balance c/d (prepaid rates) 2,500 = 85,500 ✓. **P&L = 70,000**; SOFP: accrued rent liability 16,000; prepaid rates asset 2,500.
- **Salaries and wages:** paid 150,000; opening accrual 30,000 (Dec 2003 salaries paid 5 Jan 2005 — sic); closing accrual 35,000. P&L = 150,000 − 30,000 + 35,000 = **155,000**... the book's account shows P&L 85,000 with bank 65,000 — the book's own figures are internally inconsistent here (150,000 vs 65,000 bank). The **method** is what matters: P&L = cash paid − opening accrual + closing accrual; SOFP = closing accrual as liability. State the formula and apply the question's numbers.

**The master formula (memorise):**
> **P&L charge = cash paid/received − opening prepayment/accrual + closing prepayment/accrual**
> (with signs: for expenses — add closing accrual, subtract closing prepayment; add opening prepayment, subtract opening accrual.)

pages.title: 6. Worked example – full T-accounts (Fwamba Enterprises, 31 Dec 2004, Sh. '000)
pages.markdown:
## 6. Worked example – full T-accounts (Fwamba Enterprises, 31 Dec 2004, Sh. '000)

**Insurance:** annual premium Sh. 15,000 paid 1 Jul 2004 (covers to 30 Jun 2005); total insurance paid in the year Sh. 32,000. Prepaid at year-end = 6/12 × 15,000 = **7,500**.

```
Dr                        Insurance account                       Cr
                                          '000                                      '000
Bank (premiums paid)         32,000    P&L (charge for year)        24,500
                                          Balance c/d (prepaid)       7,500
                             32,000                                     32,000
Balance b/d (prepaid asset)   7,500
```

P&L charge **24,500**; SOFP: prepayment (current asset) **7,500**.

**Commission received:** Sh. 10,000 received; Sh. 5,000 earned but not received at 31 Dec.

```
Dr                     Commission received account                Cr
                                          '000                                      '000
P&L (income for year)        15,000    Bank (received)              10,000
Balance c/d (accrued)         5,000
                             20,000                                     20,000
                                          Balance b/d (accrued asset) 5,000
```

P&L income **15,000**; SOFP: accrued income (current asset) **5,000**.

**Rent and rates** (opening: rent owing 13,000, rates prepaid 4,500; paid 65,000; closing: rent owing 16,000, rates prepaid 2,500):

```
Dr                      Rent and rates account                    Cr
                                          '000                                      '000
Balance b/d (prepaid)         4,500    Balance b/d (accrual)        13,000
Bank (paid)                  65,000    P&L (charge, bal. fig.)      70,000
Balance c/d (accrual)        16,000    Balance c/d (prepaid)         2,500
                             85,500                                     85,500
Balance b/d (prepaid asset)   2,500    Balance b/d (accrual liab.)  16,000
```

P&L charge **70,000** (the balancing figure); SOFP: accrued rent (current liability) **16,000**, prepaid rates (current asset) **2,500**. The account proves the master formula — derive it from the debits and credits: expense for the year = cash paid + closing accrual − opening accrual + opening prepayment − closing prepayment = 65,000 + 16,000 − 13,000 + 4,500 − 2,500 = **70,000** ✓. Memorise it in this direction: **add closing accruals and opening prepayments; subtract opening accruals and closing prepayments.**

pages.title: 7. Common exam traps
pages.markdown:
## 7. Common exam traps

1. **Principal vs interest** on loans — only interest touches P&L.
2. Accrued expense = **liability**; prepaid expense = **asset**; accrued income = **asset**; prepaid income = **liability**. Draw the 2×2 grid in the margin.
3. Rent received in advance is **not** income — it is a liability until earned.
4. In ledger accounts, the accrual/prepayment **c/d** goes on the opposite side to the P&L transfer; the **b/d** reverses it next period.
5. Insurance/rates questions: time-apportion the annual premium (months before/after year-end).

pages.title: Key terms (flashcards)
pages.markdown:
## Key terms (flashcards)

- **Liability** – Present obligation from past events; settled by outflow of resources.
- **Trade payables** – Amounts owed to suppliers/creditors; current if due within 12 months.
- **Bank overdraft** – Negative bank balance; current liability (credit balance in cash book).
- **Accrued expense** – Incurred but unpaid at year-end; current liability.
- **Prepaid expense** – Paid in advance; current asset.
- **Accrued income** – Earned but not received; current asset.
- **Prepaid (unearned) income** – Received in advance; current liability.
- **Loan principal** – Amount borrowed; repaid via SOFP only, never an expense.
- **Interest expense** – Cost of borrowing; charged to P&L (accrue if unpaid).
- **Bills payable** – Accepted bills of exchange; reduce trade creditors.

pages.title: Module summary
pages.markdown:
## Module summary

Liabilities are present obligations from past events — trade payables, overdrafts, loans, accruals and prepaid income. Loan receipts and repayments are statement-of-financial-position movements; only interest touches profit or loss. The accruals concept puts each period's true cost in its own period: P&L = cash paid + closing accrual − opening accrual + opening prepayment − closing prepayment. Accrued expenses and prepaid income are liabilities; prepaid expenses and accrued income are assets.

pages.title: Exam day tips
pages.markdown:
## Exam day tips

- For accruals/prepayments, draw the expense/income T-account with the four lines (b/d, cash, P&L, c/d) — the balancing figure is always the P&L charge or the SOFP balance.
- Loan questions: split every instalment into principal and interest first.
- Control-account questions: remember bills payable/dishonoured bills and contras — they are the "twist" items.

chapters.module: Correction of Errors and Suspense Accounts

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# 01-types-of-errors

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. Define an accounting error and explain why a balanced trial balance does not guarantee error-free books.
2. Classify errors into those that affect and those that do not affect the agreement of the trial balance.
3. Identify and explain the seven types of errors not disclosed by the trial balance: omission, principle, commission, compensating errors, original entry, complete reversal of entries, and transposition.
4. Prepare journal entries (with narratives) to correct each type of error.
5. Apply the "doubling rule" for complete reversals of entries.
6. Distinguish transposition errors and use the divisibility-by-nine test to trace them.

---

pages.title: 1. Why a Balanced Trial Balance Is Not Proof of Accuracy
pages.markdown:
## 1. Why a Balanced Trial Balance Is Not Proof of Accuracy

A trial balance is a statement of proof done arithmetically to prove that proper double entry was observed when recording transactions. The working assumption is simple: if the total of the debit balances equals the total of the credit balances, the double entry is arithmetically correct.

But that is all it proves — arithmetical accuracy. A trial balance will balance even when serious accounting errors exist, because some errors keep debits and credits equal. KASNEB therefore divides all bookkeeping errors into two basic classes:

- **Errors which do not affect the trial balance totals** — the trial balance still balances.
- **Errors which affect the trial balance totals** — the trial balance fails to agree and a suspense account is needed (covered in Lesson 2).

The golden rule for correction: **the correction of every accounting error must be journalised by way of the General Journal**, and every correction must be supported by a clear narrative explaining what error is being corrected. Examiners award marks for the narrative — never omit it.

pages.title: 2. The Seven Errors That Leave the Trial Balance Balanced
pages.markdown:
## 2. The Seven Errors That Leave the Trial Balance Balanced

### 2.1 Error of Omission

An error of omission occurs when a transaction is **completely omitted** from the books of account. Neither the debit nor the credit is recorded, so debits and credits remain equal.

*Example:* A motor van bought for cash at Sh.90,000 is recorded nowhere — neither the motor vehicle account is debited nor the cash account credited. The trial balance still balances.

**Correction:** Simply record the omitted transaction through the journal:

```
Dr. Motor vehicle account        90,000
    Cr. Cash account                          90,000
(Being motor van purchased for cash, omitted from the books; error now corrected)
```

### 2.2 Error of Principle

An error of principle occurs when a transaction is entered in the **wrong class of account**, but double entry is still observed. Because the debit and credit are both recorded (just in the wrong account class), the trial balance is unaffected.

*Example:* Furniture (a fixed asset) bought for Sh.200,000 cash is debited to the **purchases** account instead of the furniture account, and cash is credited correctly. Purchases is a trading account item; furniture is a non-current asset. Double entry was observed, so the trial balance balances — but the financial statements will be wrong (assets understated, cost of sales overstated).

**Correction:**

```
Dr. Furniture account           200,000
    Cr. Purchases account                    200,000
(To correct error of principle: purchase of fixed asset wrongly debited to purchases account)
```

### 2.3 Error of Commission

An error of commission occurs when the **correct amount is entered in the wrong personal account**, even though the account is in the correct class. For example, a credit sale of Sh.20,000 to D. Waithaka is posted to the account of P. Waithaka in the sales ledger. Both are debtors, so the trial balance still agrees.

**Correction:** Simply transfer the amount between the two personal accounts:

```
Dr. D. Waithaka account          20,000
    Cr. P. Waithaka account                   20,000
(To transfer credit sale wrongly posted to P. Waithaka to the correct account of D. Waithaka)
```

Note: the sales account is untouched, and because both personal accounts sit in the same sales ledger, the trial balance is still balanced after correction.

### 2.4 Compensating Errors

Compensating errors are errors that **cancel each other out** — an error that overstates both the credits and the debits, or understates both, by the same amount.

*Example:* Purchases returns are overstated by Sh.2,000 and sales returns are overstated by Sh.2,000. Purchases returns appear on the credit side of the trial balance and sales returns on the debit side, so the two overstatements cancel out.

**Correction:**

```
Dr. Purchases returns account     2,000
    Cr. Sales returns account                  2,000
(To correct compensating errors: purchases returns and sales returns both overstated by Sh.2,000)
```

pages.title: 2. The Seven Errors That Leave the Trial Balance Balanced (continued)
pages.markdown:
## 2. The Seven Errors That Leave the Trial Balance Balanced (continued)

### 2.5 Error of Original Entry

An error of original entry occurs when the **original figure is incorrect**, yet double entry is observed using that incorrect figure. The figure may be understated or overstated.

*Example:* Purchases worth Sh.20,000 are recorded as Sh.200,000 in **both** the purchases account and the cash account.

The wrong entry was:

```
Dr. Purchases       200,000
    Cr. Cash                     200,000
```

The correct entry should have been:

```
Dr. Purchases        20,000
    Cr. Cash                      20,000
```

**Correction** (for the excess of Sh.180,000):

```
Dr. Cash account                180,000
    Cr. Purchases account                    180,000
(To correct error of original entry: purchases of Sh.20,000 recorded as Sh.200,000; excess now reversed)
```

### 2.6 Complete Reversal of Entries

A complete reversal of entries occurs when the correct accounts and the correct amounts are used, but **each item is shown on the wrong side** of its account. Because a debit is still matched by an equal credit, the trial balance balances.

*Example — goods taken by the owner for personal use:* Sh.1,250 of goods are taken for own use. The correct entry is:

```
Dr. Drawings account       1,250
    Cr. Purchases account               1,250
```

But the bookkeeper reversed it completely:

```
Dr. Purchases account      1,250
    Cr. Drawings account                1,250
```

**Correction** is done in two stages: (1) cancel the wrong entry, (2) record the correct entry:

```
Dr. Drawings account       1,250        (to cancel the wrong entry)
    Cr. Purchases account               1,250

Dr. Drawings account       1,250        (to record the correct entry)
    Cr. Purchases account               1,250
```

Because both stages credit purchases and debit drawings, the two entries are combined into one entry with a **doubled amount**:

```
Dr. Drawings account       2,500
    Cr. Purchases account               2,500
(To correct complete reversal of entries: goods for own use Sh.1,250 debited to purchases
 and credited to drawings; amount doubled — one entry to cancel, one to record correctly)
```

**The doubling rule:** when correcting a complete reversal, double the figure. A single credit of the original amount would merely cancel the initial wrong debit; the second equal credit then enters the credit that should have been there all along.

### 2.7 Transposition Error

A transposition error is a special type of error of original entry. It occurs when the **wrong sequence of individual characters** in a figure is entered — for example, entering Sh.870 as Sh.780. It is very difficult to trace, but there is a classic diagnostic test:

> If a transposition occurs on **only one side** of the entry, the difference between the debit and credit columns of the trial balance will be a number **divisible by nine**.

*Example:* Cash sales of Sh.9,260 are entered as Sh.6,290 in both the cash book and the sales ledger.

The wrong entry was:

pages.title: 2. The Seven Errors That Leave the Trial Balance Balanced (continued)
pages.markdown:
## 2. The Seven Errors That Leave the Trial Balance Balanced (continued)

```
Dr. Cash        6,290
    Cr. Sales               6,290
```

**Correction** (for the shortfall of Sh.9,260 − Sh.6,290 = Sh.2,970):

```
Dr. Cash account             2,970
    Cr. Sales account                      2,970
(To correct transposition error: cash sales Sh.9,260 entered as Sh.6,290; shortfall now recorded)
```

Note that in this example the same wrong figure was used on both sides, so the trial balance was unaffected. But had the error occurred on one side only (e.g., Sh.9,260 debited to cash and Sh.6,290 credited to sales), the trial balance difference would be Sh.2,970 — and 2,970 ÷ 9 = 330 exactly. Examiners love asking you to spot this.

pages.title: 3. Worked Example: Journal Corrections With Narratives
pages.markdown:
## 3. Worked Example: Journal Corrections With Narratives

**Question (KASNEB style):** Show the journal entries required to correct the following errors. Narratives must be shown.

1. Commissions received of Sh.44,000 had been credited to the rent receivable account.
2. Bank charges of Sh.3,850 had been debited to the rent account.
3. A payment of sundry expenses by cheque of Sh.1,150 was completely omitted from the books.
4. Purchase of fixtures of Sh.23,700 had been entered in the purchases account.

**Solution:**

```
1.  Dr. Rent receivable account          44,000
        Cr. Commissions received account              44,000
    (To correct error of principle: commission received wrongly credited to rent receivable)

2.  Dr. Bank charges account              3,850
        Cr. Rent account                               3,850
    (To correct error of commission/principle: bank charges wrongly debited to rent account)

3.  Dr. Sundry expenses account           1,150
        Cr. Bank account                               1,150
    (To record payment of sundry expenses omitted from the books)

4.  Dr. Fixtures account                 23,700
        Cr. Purchases account                         23,700
    (To correct error of principle: purchase of fixtures wrongly debited to purchases account)
```

Each entry balances (debits = credits), each names the error type, and each narrative would earn its mark in the exam.

![Error type classification chart](https://jorjhskqykkajcaiweqn.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/course-media/ca11/m04-correction-of-errors-and-suspense-accounts/illustrations/error-types-classification.png)

pages.title: 4. Common Exam Traps
pages.markdown:
## 4. Common Exam Traps

1. **"The trial balance balances, so there are no errors."** False — this is the single most tested misconception in this topic. Memorise all seven error types that leave the trial balance intact.
2. **Correcting without a narrative.** KASNEB explicitly demands narratives ("Narratives must be shown"). A journal without a narrative loses marks.
3. **Forgetting the doubling rule.** For complete reversals, a single entry of the original amount only cancels the error; you must double it to also record the correct entry.
4. **Using the suspense account for these errors.** Errors in this lesson do **not** need a suspense account — both sides of the correction are ordinary ledger accounts. Suspense is only for errors that break the trial balance agreement.
5. **Confusing commission with principle.** Commission = wrong *person* within the *same class*; principle = wrong *class* of account. The distinction determines which accounts appear in the correction.
6. **Transposition test direction.** The divisibility-by-nine test only applies when the transposition affects one side of the entry (trial balance fails to agree). If both sides carry the same wrong figure, the trial balance still balances.

pages.title: 5. Key Terms (Flashcards)
pages.markdown:
## 5. Key Terms (Flashcards)

- **Trial balance** — A statement prepared arithmetically to prove that proper double entry was observed; the debit totals must equal the credit totals.
- **Error of omission** — A transaction completely omitted from the books; neither debit nor credit recorded.
- **Error of principle** — A transaction entered in the wrong class of account while double entry is still observed.
- **Error of commission** — The correct amount entered in the wrong personal account within the correct class.
- **Compensating errors** — Two or more errors that cancel each other out by equal and opposite amounts.
- **Error of original entry** — The original figure is wrong, but double entry is observed with the wrong figure.
- **Complete reversal of entries** — Correct accounts and amounts, but each item posted to the wrong side; corrected by doubling the amount.
- **Transposition error** — Digits of a figure entered in the wrong sequence; a one-sided transposition gives a trial balance difference divisible by nine.
- **Journal narrative** — The written explanation accompanying a journal entry, stating which error is being corrected and how.
- **General Journal** — The book in which all corrections of errors must be journalised before posting to the ledger.

pages.title: 6. Lesson Summary
pages.markdown:
## 6. Lesson Summary

- A balanced trial balance proves only arithmetical accuracy, not the absence of errors.
- Seven error types do not affect trial balance agreement: omission, principle, commission, compensating, original entry, complete reversal, and transposition.
- All corrections pass through the General Journal with a narrative; every correction must balance (debits = credits).
- Complete reversals are corrected with a doubled amount (cancel + re-record in one entry).
- Transposition errors on one side only produce a trial balance difference divisible by nine.

pages.title: 7. Exam Day Tips
pages.markdown:
## 7. Exam Day Tips

- When a question says "the trial balance still balanced" or "the trial balance agreed", immediately think of the seven errors in this lesson — and rule out the suspense account.
- Write the wrong entry and the correct entry side by side before drafting your correction; it makes the required journal obvious and avoids sign errors.
- Always state the *type* of error in your narrative (e.g., "to correct error of principle...") — examiners reward precise terminology.
- For "show the ledger accounts after correction" follow-ups, post your journal entries and balance each T-account; the two sides of every correction keep the ledger in balance automatically.

---

*Next: Lesson 2 — Suspense Accounts and Corrections, where we handle the errors that DO break the trial balance.*

chapters.module: Correction of Errors and Suspense Accounts

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# 02-suspense-accounts-and-corrections

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. Explain when a suspense account is opened and how the trial balance difference is posted to it.
2. Identify errors that affect the agreement of the trial balance (one-sided entries, wrong corresponding entries, casting errors).
3. Pass journal entries that correct errors through the suspense account.
4. Prepare a fully balanced suspense account.
5. Prepare a statement of corrected net profit (and corrected gross profit) after discovering errors.
6. Explain why the suspense account must not be used to balance the trial balance unless the examiner specifically requires it.

---

pages.title: 1. When the Trial Balance Fails to Agree
pages.markdown:
## 1. When the Trial Balance Fails to Agree

Lesson 1 dealt with errors that leave the trial balance balanced. But some errors break the double-entry equality — for example:

- **Failure to enter a corresponding entry** for every debit or credit made (one side of an entry completely missing).
- **Making a wrong corresponding entry** — e.g., cash sales of Sh.20,000 are correctly debited to the cash book, but the sales account is credited with only Sh.2,000. The credit side of the trial balance is then understated by Sh.18,000.
- **Casting (addition) errors** in day books — e.g., the purchases day book undercast by Sh.11,200 or the sales day book overcast by Sh.3,000.
- **Posting to the wrong side** of the correct account, or entering an amount on one side only.

Because the error may take a long time to identify, the accountant is allowed to open a temporary account called the **suspense account** and post the trial balance difference to it, so that the books can be closed and draft financial statements prepared while the investigation continues.

**The rule for opening it:** post the difference to the side that makes the trial balance agree.

- If the **debit side exceeds** the credit side by Sh.100,000, the suspense account is given a **credit balance** of Sh.100,000.
- If the **credit side exceeds** the debit side, the suspense account is given a **debit balance**.

When the errors are later found, journal entries are passed **against the suspense account** until its balance is cleared — the suspense account then disappears from the books.

> **Exam caution (straight from the study text):** the suspense account should not be used to balance the trial balance unless the examiner specifically asks you to do so.

pages.title: 2. Journal Corrections Through the Suspense Account
pages.markdown:
## 2. Journal Corrections Through the Suspense Account

The technique is identical to Lesson 1 — every correction goes through the General Journal with a narrative — except that one side of each correction is the suspense account, standing in for the missing or wrong half of the original entry.

Taking the sales example above: cash sales of Sh.20,000 were debited to cash, but sales was credited with only Sh.2,000. The suspense account was opened with a credit balance of Sh.18,000. On discovery:

```
Dr. Suspense account             18,000
    Cr. Sales account                         18,000
(To correct the error understating the credit side of the trial balance: sales credited with Sh.2,000 instead of Sh.20,000)
```

The debit to suspense reduces its credit balance; when all errors are corrected, the suspense account balances to nil.

pages.title: 3. Fully Worked Example: Suspense Account + Corrected Net Profit
pages.markdown:
## 3. Fully Worked Example: Suspense Account + Corrected Net Profit

**Question (KASNEB style):** The trial balance extracted from the books of J. Kamau as at 31 December 2025 failed to agree. The debit side totalled Sh.2,450,000 and the credit side Sh.2,380,000. The difference was posted to a suspense account and draft financial statements were prepared, showing a net profit of Sh.512,000.

The following errors were later discovered:

1. Cash sales of Sh.50,000 had been correctly debited to the cash account, but the sales account was credited with Sh.5,000 only.
2. A cheque for Sh.25,000 received from W. Mwangi, a debtor, had been debited in the cash book, but no other entry was made.
3. Motor vehicle repairs of Sh.30,000 had been posted to the motor vehicle account.

**Required:**
(a) Journal entries to correct the errors.
(b) The suspense account, fully balanced.
(c) A statement of corrected net profit.

### Solution

**(a) Journal entries**

The trial balance difference is Sh.2,450,000 − Sh.2,380,000 = **Sh.70,000** (debit exceeds credit), so the suspense account was opened with a **credit balance of Sh.70,000**.

```
Dr. Suspense account              45,000
    Cr. Sales account                          45,000
(To correct sales understated by Sh.45,000, i.e. Sh.50,000 − Sh.5,000; credit side of trial balance now corrected)

Dr. Suspense account              25,000
    Cr. W. Mwangi (debtor) account             25,000
(To record receipt from debtor omitted from the personal account; error of one-sided entry now corrected)

Dr. Motor vehicle repairs account  30,000
    Cr. Motor vehicle account                   30,000
(To correct error of principle: repairs posted to the motor vehicle asset account; no suspense entry needed)
```

Check each entry balances: 45,000 = 45,000; 25,000 = 25,000; 30,000 = 30,000. ✓

Note that error 3 does not touch the suspense account: both the repairs (expense) and the motor vehicle (asset) carry debit balances, so the trial balance was unaffected — exactly the Lesson 1 logic.

**(b) Suspense account**

```
                          Suspense Account
                   Sh.                              Sh.
Sales                   45,000   Balance b/d             70,000
W. Mwangi               25,000
                        70,000                          70,000
```

The suspense account is fully cleared — total debits Sh.70,000 equal total credits Sh.70,000, leaving a nil balance. The suspense account now disappears from the books. ✓

**(c) Statement of corrected net profit**

Only errors affecting profit change the net profit figure:

- Error 1: sales were understated by Sh.45,000 → profit increases by Sh.45,000.
- Error 2: the debtor receipt affects only the statement of financial position (bank vs. debtor) → no profit effect.
- Error 3: Sh.30,000 wrongly capitalised as a motor vehicle must now be expensed as repairs → profit decreases by Sh.30,000.

pages.title: 3. Fully Worked Example: Suspense Account + Corrected Net Profit (continued)
pages.markdown:
## 3. Fully Worked Example: Suspense Account + Corrected Net Profit (continued)

```
            J. Kamau — Statement of Corrected Net Profit
                        for the year ended 31 December 2025
                                                Sh.
Net profit as per draft accounts           512,000
Add: Sales understated                      45,000
Less: Motor repairs wrongly capitalised    (30,000)
Corrected net profit                       527,000
```

**Exam technique:** always ask of each error, "does this touch the income statement?" If it only moves amounts within the statement of financial position (bank, debtors, creditors, suspense), it leaves profit unchanged.

pages.title: 4. Corrected Gross Profit — A Further Twist
pages.markdown:
## 4. Corrected Gross Profit — A Further Twist

Sometimes the examiner asks for a **statement of corrected gross profit** as well as corrected net profit (as in the Bernard Masita revision question). The logic is the same, but restricted to trading items:

- Items affecting gross profit: sales, purchases, returns inwards/outwards, carriage inwards, opening and closing stock, goods taken for own use (drawings in the form of goods reduce purchases).
- Items affecting only net profit: salaries, rent, discounts, stationery, bad debts, depreciation.

Work through the errors one by one and sort them into the "gross profit" bucket or the "net profit only" bucket before adjusting.

pages.title: 5. A Second Mini-Example: Casting Errors
pages.markdown:
## 5. A Second Mini-Example: Casting Errors

Casting (totalling) errors are the most common suspense-account triggers in KASNEB exams.

- **Purchases day book undercast by Sh.11,200** → purchases (debit) understated → trial balance debit side short by Sh.11,200. Correction: `Dr. Purchases 11,200 / Cr. Suspense 11,200`. Profit falls by Sh.11,200.
- **Sales day book overcast by Sh.3,000** → sales (credit) overstated → trial balance credit side too high by Sh.3,000. Correction: `Dr. Sales 3,000 / Cr. Suspense 3,000`. Profit falls by Sh.3,000.
- **Returns outwards overcast by Sh.5,600** → returns outwards (credit) overstated. Correction: `Dr. Returns outwards 5,600 / Cr. Suspense 5,600`. Profit falls by Sh.5,600 (cost of sales rises).

Notice the pattern: the suspense account always takes the opposite side to the corrected ledger account, and casting corrections always need suspense because the trial balance totals were wrong.

pages.title: 6. Common Exam Traps
pages.markdown:
## 6. Common Exam Traps

1. **Opening the suspense balance on the wrong side.** Debit exceeds credit → suspense gets a *credit* balance (it plugs the credit side). Say it as a mantra: "the suspense balance goes on the *short* side."
2. **Leaving a balance on the suspense account.** After all corrections, the suspense account must total to zero. If yours does not, one of your correction entries is wrong — recheck each one.
3. **Adjusting profit for non-profit errors.** Debtor/creditor/bank-only corrections do not change net profit. Only income-statement items do.
4. **Double-counting the suspense balance in the corrected profit statement.** The suspense account is a statement-of-financial-position item; it never appears in the profit adjustment.
5. **Forgetting that some discovered errors need no suspense entry.** Always test each error first: "did this error break the trial balance agreement?" If not, correct it directly between the two ledger accounts.
6. **Discount mix-ups.** Discount received posted as discount allowed (or vice versa) is a favourite: cancel the wrong posting, then record the correct one — the suspense entry is the difference between the two sides.

![Suspense account flow diagram](https://jorjhskqykkajcaiweqn.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/course-media/ca11/m04-correction-of-errors-and-suspense-accounts/illustrations/suspense-account-flow.png)

pages.title: 7. Key Terms (Flashcards)
pages.markdown:
## 7. Key Terms (Flashcards)

- **Suspense account** — A temporary account opened to hold the trial balance difference while errors are investigated; cleared by correction journals once errors are found.
- **Trial balance difference** — The amount by which the debit and credit columns disagree; posted to the suspense account on the short side.
- **Casting error** — An addition mistake (undercast or overcast) in a day book or ledger account total.
- **Undercast** — A total added up to less than the true figure.
- **Overcast** — A total added up to more than the true figure.
- **One-sided entry error** — An error where only the debit or only the credit of a transaction was recorded.
- **Statement of corrected net profit** — A statement adjusting the draft net profit for the profit effect of each discovered error.
- **Draft financial statements** — Statements prepared before all errors are found, containing the suspense account balance.

pages.title: 8. Lesson Summary
pages.markdown:
## 8. Lesson Summary

- Errors that break trial balance agreement (missing one side of an entry, wrong corresponding entries, casting errors) require a suspense account.
- The suspense account takes the trial balance difference on the short side (debit exceeds credit → credit balance).
- Every correction is journalised with a narrative; one leg of the entry is the suspense account.
- When all errors are corrected, the suspense account must balance to nil.
- The statement of corrected net profit adjusts the draft profit only for errors affecting income or expenses.

pages.title: 9. Exam Day Tips
pages.markdown:
## 9. Exam Day Tips

- Start every suspense question by computing the difference and stating the opening suspense balance with its side — it anchors all subsequent entries.
- After posting all corrections, total the suspense account as a self-check: it must be nil.
- For the corrected profit statement, annotate each error with "+" or "−" for profit before writing the statement; it prevents sign errors under pressure.
- If the question also asks for corrected *gross* profit, filter the errors to trading items only (sales, purchases, returns, carriage inwards, stock, drawings in kind).

---

*Module complete. Test yourself with the module quiz, then move on to Module 5 — Financial Statements of a Sole Trader.*

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# 01-income-statement-of-a-sole-trader

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. Define a sole trader and explain the purpose of the income statement.
2. Distinguish the trading section (gross profit) from the profit and loss section (net profit).
3. Compute cost of sales from opening stock, purchases, returns, carriage inwards and closing stock.
4. Classify items correctly between the trading account and the profit and loss account.
5. Prepare a trading and profit and loss account in vertical format from given data.
6. Treat special items correctly: abnormal losses, goods in transit, goods on approval, and free samples.

---

pages.title: 1. The Sole Trader and the Need for Financial Statements
pages.markdown:
## 1. The Sole Trader and the Need for Financial Statements

A sole trader — also called a sole proprietorship — is a business owned and run by one individual, with no legal distinction between the owner and the business. You own it entirely, you grow it, and its success or failure rests on you. You are entitled to all the profit it makes.

At the end of each financial year, every business must answer one question: **did we make a profit or a loss?** This is done in two stages:

1. **Finding gross profit (or gross loss)** — in the trading account section.
2. **Finding net profit (or net loss)** — in the profit and loss account section.

The trial balance provides the essential input. In practice the two sections are combined into a single report — the **income statement** — but examiners still expect you to know which items belong to each stage.

pages.title: 2. Stage 1: Determining Gross Profit
pages.markdown:
## 2. Stage 1: Determining Gross Profit

Gross profit is the difference between the **sale proceeds of the period** and the **cost of the goods actually sold**. No deduction of any kind — general, administrative, or selling and distribution expenses — is made at this stage. If sale proceeds exceed the cost of goods sold, there is a gross profit; if cost exceeds proceeds, a gross loss.

### Items debited (the cost side)

- **Opening stock** — the value of goods on hand at the end of the previous year, which becomes the opening stock of the current year.
- **Purchases** — goods bought for resale, cash or credit. Adjust for:
  - purchases of **capital assets** wrongly included (deduct them);
  - goods taken for **personal use/drawings** (exclude — treat as drawings);
  - goods **in transit** at year-end (debit stock-in-transit, credit supplier);
  - goods received on **consignment, on approval or hire purchase** (exclude);
  - cost of goods **sent on consignment** (deduct from purchases).
- **Returns outwards (purchases returns)** — shown as a deduction from purchases (or on the credit side).
- **Direct expenses** — expenses incurred in purchasing, procuring or producing the goods and bringing them to the point of sale. The classic exam item is **carriage inwards**.

### Items credited (the revenue side)

- **Sales** — cash and credit sales of the goods the business deals in. Exclude: sale of old fixed assets, goods sent on approval (until approved), free samples, and any sales tax included in the figure.
- **Returns inwards (sales returns)** — deducted from sales (or shown on the debit side).
- **Abnormal loss of stock** — stock lost through fire, theft or accident is credited in full to the trading account, because the trading account is prepared under *normal* conditions and has no place for abnormal events. (The loss itself is then dealt with in the profit and loss account.)
- **Closing stock** — goods unsold at year-end, valued at **cost or market price, whichever is lower**. The trial balance normally does *not* include closing stock, so it is brought in by: `Dr. Closing stock account / Cr. Income statement`. If closing stock already appears in the trial balance, it goes **only** to the statement of financial position.

### The cost-of-sales formula (memorise this)

```
Opening stock
+ Purchases
+ Carriage inwards (direct expenses)
− Returns outwards
= Cost of goods available for sale
− Closing stock
= COST OF SALES
```

```
Net sales (sales − returns inwards) − Cost of sales = GROSS PROFIT
```

pages.title: 3. Worked Example: Trading Account
pages.markdown:
## 3. Worked Example: Trading Account

**Question:** From the following details, draw up the trading account of Mr. Karanja for the year ended 31 December 2025, his first year in business.

| Item | Sh. |
|---|---|
| Carriage inwards | 134,000 |
| Returns outwards | 99,000 |
| Returns inwards | 178,000 |
| Sales | 7,748,400 |
| Purchases | 6,666,600 |
| Stock at 31 December 2025 | 1,497,800 |

**Solution:**

```
                                    Mr. Karanja
                 Trading Account for the year ended 31 December 2025
                                                    Sh.            Sh.
Sales                                            7,748,400
Less: Returns inwards                             (178,000)
Net sales                                                        7,570,400
Less: Cost of sales
  Purchases                          6,666,600
  Add: Carriage inwards                 134,000
                                     6,800,600
  Less: Returns outwards                (99,000)
  Cost of goods available for sale   6,701,600
  Less: Closing stock               (1,497,800)
  Cost of sales                                                 (5,203,800)
Gross profit                                                     2,366,600
```

Check: 7,570,400 − 5,203,800 = 2,366,600. ✓ (There is no opening stock — it is his first year in business.)

pages.title: 4. Stage 2: Determining Net Profit
pages.markdown:
## 4. Stage 2: Determining Net Profit

After gross profit is found, all remaining **indirect** expenses and losses are charged on the debit side, and all other incomes on the credit side:

**Debited (expenses and losses):**
- Management/administrative expenses — office salaries, office rent, printing and stationery, telephone.
- Selling and distribution expenses — salesmen's salaries and commission, advertising, packaging, **carriage outwards**, bad debts.
- Maintenance expenses — repairs and renewals of office fixed assets.
- Financial expenses — interest on loans, bank charges, discount allowed.
- Abnormal losses — e.g., stock lost by fire not covered by insurance, loss on sale of machinery.
- Depreciation of non-current assets.

**Credited (other incomes):**
- Gross profit brought down.
- Other income — discount received, commission received.
- Non-trading income — interest on bank deposits, dividends, rent of property let out, profit on sale of fixed assets.
- Abnormal gains — e.g., profit on sale of a fixed asset (shown separately).

Net profit = total credits − total debits. If debits exceed credits, it is a net loss. The balancing figure is entered on the smaller side, after which both sides agree.

pages.title: 5. Special Treatments Examiners Love
pages.markdown:
## 5. Special Treatments Examiners Love

- **Carriage inwards vs. carriage outwards:** carriage *inwards* is a direct expense (trading account, part of cost of sales); carriage *outwards* is a selling expense (profit and loss account). Mixing them up is a classic mark-loser.
- **Returns:** returns *inwards* reduce sales; returns *outwards* reduce purchases. Always net them off — never add them.
- **Abnormal loss of stock:** credit the trading account in full (normal conditions only), then charge the loss to the profit and loss account. If insured, recognise the insurance claim as an asset until received.
- **Goods sent on approval:** not a sale until the customer approves. Cancel the sale (Dr. Sales / Cr. Debtors at selling price) and add the goods back to closing stock at cost.
- **Free samples:** advertisement expense — `Dr. Advertisement / Cr. Purchases`, then charge advertisement to the profit and loss account.
- **Drawings in kind:** goods taken by the owner reduce purchases at cost (`Dr. Drawings / Cr. Purchases`).

![Income statement format](https://jorjhskqykkajcaiweqn.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/course-media/ca11/m05-financial-statements-of-a-sole-trader/illustrations/income-statement-format.png)

pages.title: 6. Common Exam Traps
pages.markdown:
## 6. Common Exam Traps

1. **Carriage inwards vs. carriage outwards** — the single most confused pair in this topic. Inwards = cost of sales; outwards = selling expense.
2. **Adding returns instead of deducting them** — returns inwards reduce sales; returns outwards reduce purchases.
3. **Putting closing stock in the trial balance section** — closing stock from *additional information* is credited to the trading account AND shown as a current asset. (If it were already in the trial balance, it would go to the statement of financial position only.)
4. **Charging indirect expenses in the trading account** — salaries, rent, insurance and depreciation belong below gross profit, never above it.
5. **Forgetting that sales excludes fixed-asset disposals** — selling an old van is not "sales"; any profit or loss goes to the profit and loss account separately.
6. **Treating abnormal losses as normal cost of sales** — they are credited out of the trading account and charged below the line.

pages.title: 7. Key Terms (Flashcards)
pages.markdown:
## 7. Key Terms (Flashcards)

- **Sole trader** — A business owned and run by one individual with no legal distinction between owner and business.
- **Income statement** — The combined trading and profit and loss account showing gross profit and net profit for a period.
- **Gross profit** — Net sales minus cost of sales; profit before deducting indirect expenses.
- **Net profit** — Gross profit plus other incomes minus all indirect expenses; the final result for the period.
- **Cost of sales** — Opening stock + purchases + direct expenses − returns outwards − closing stock.
- **Direct expenses** — Expenses of purchasing/procuring goods and bringing them to the point of sale (e.g., carriage inwards).
- **Returns inwards** — Goods returned by customers; deducted from sales.
- **Returns outwards** — Goods returned to suppliers; deducted from purchases.
- **Abnormal loss** — Stock lost through fire, theft or accident; credited to the trading account and charged to profit and loss.
- **Closing stock** — Unsold goods at year-end, valued at cost or market price, whichever is lower.

pages.title: 8. Lesson Summary
pages.markdown:
## 8. Lesson Summary

- The income statement answers in two stages: gross profit (trading section) then net profit (profit and loss section).
- Cost of sales = opening stock + purchases + carriage inwards − returns outwards − closing stock.
- Only direct items sit above gross profit; all indirect expenses and other incomes sit below it.
- Special items — abnormal losses, approval sales, free samples, drawings in kind — each have a fixed treatment you must memorise.

pages.title: 9. Exam Day Tips
pages.markdown:
## 9. Exam Day Tips

- Write the cost-of-sales formula at the top of your answer page before you start — it prevents omission errors under pressure.
- Always compute **net sales** and **net purchases** first; then the rest is mechanical.
- Label every figure (Sh.) and show workings for closing stock and adjustments — method marks are generous.
- In combined income statements, draw a clear line (or subtotal) at gross profit so the examiner sees both stages.

---

*Next: Lesson 2 — the Statement of Financial Position: grouping, marshalling, and the accounting equation in exam format.*
