## Key Terms

- **Cost of sales (manufacturer)** — opening finished goods + cost of production − closing finished goods.
- **Net sales** — sales less returns inwards.
- **Manufacturing profit add-back** — credited after gross profit when transfer is above cost.
- **Three inventories** — raw materials, work in progress, finished goods; all current assets.

pages.title: Module Summary
pages.markdown:
## Module Summary

- The manufacturer's income statement substitutes cost of production for purchases and uses finished-goods stocks for cost of sales.
- Manufacturing profit (transfer above cost) is added after gross profit; unrealised profit in closing stock is provided for so stock is carried at cost.
- Expenses are apportioned: factory → manufacturing account; administration, selling/distribution, finance → profit and loss.
- The SFP shows raw materials, WIP and finished goods separately under current assets.

pages.title: Exam Day Tips
pages.markdown:
## Exam Day Tips

1. Always label which stock you mean — "finished goods" — markers penalise bare "stock" figures in the trading section.
2. Finish the manufacturing account *before* starting the income statement; carry the transfer figure across unchanged.
3. The allowance for doubtful debts movement (new − old) is the P&L charge — compute it as a working, never by instinct.
4. Prove net profit with the credits-minus-debits check shown above; it takes thirty seconds and catches classification slips.
5. In the SFP, deduct the allowance from receivables on the face — not in a working.

chapters.lesson: Single Entry and the Capital Comparison Method

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# Single Entry and the Capital Comparison Method

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

1. Explain why small businesses keep incomplete records and describe the features of the "single entry" approach.
2. Distinguish pure, simple and quasi single entry.
3. Ascertain profit by the capital comparison (net worth) method, adjusting for drawings and fresh capital introduced.
4. Identify drawings and fresh capital hidden in cash records.

---

pages.title: 1. Why Incomplete Records Exist
pages.markdown:
## 1. Why Incomplete Records Exist

Very often, small sole proprietorships and partnerships in Kenya — the kiosk, the salon, the small agrovet — do **not** maintain a full double-entry system. They may record only cash transactions and personal (debtors/creditors) accounts, or keep no records of many transactions at all. Yet at year-end the owner wants to know: *did I make a profit, and what is my business worth?*

The term **"single entry system"** is popular but misleading — **there is no such system**. What exists is a family of **incomplete records**: hybrid methods where some transactions get double entries, some get one entry, and some get none. The accountant's task is to establish linkages among the fragments and finalise the accounts.

### Features of incomplete records

- Inaccurate, unscientific and unsystematic recording.
- Generally **no record of real and nominal accounts**; usually only cash and personal accounts are kept.
- The cash book **mixes business and personal** transactions of the owner.
- No uniformity — the "system" differs from firm to firm.
- Profit is only an **estimate**; no dependable balance sheet can be drawn directly.

### Three types of incomplete records

1. **Pure single entry** — only *personal* accounts are maintained. No information on cash, sales or purchases. Exists only on paper; no practical use.
2. **Simple single entry** — personal accounts **plus a cash book** are kept (on double-entry principles), but cash-book postings go *only* to personal accounts; no nominal or real accounts exist in the ledger.
3. **Quasi single entry** — personal accounts, cash book **and some subsidiary books** (sales book, purchases book, bills books). Discounts are entered only in personal accounts. Some scattered expense information (wages, rent) is also available. **This is the type actually used** as a substitute for double entry — and the type KASNEB examines.

---

pages.title: 2. Ascertaining Profit by Capital Comparison
pages.markdown:
## 2. Ascertaining Profit by Capital Comparison

When revenue and expense detail is unavailable, a profit and loss account cannot be built. Instead, compare **capital (net worth)** at two dates:

```
Closing capital − Opening capital = Profit (before adjustments)
```

Capital grows with profit and fresh investment, and shrinks with losses and drawings. So the full computation is:

```
Capital at the end                                            xxx
Add: Drawings (withdrawals reduce capital, so add back)       xxx
Less: Fresh capital introduced (increases capital)            (xxx)
                                                              xxx
Less: Capital at the beginning                               (xxx)
PROFIT FOR THE PERIOD                                         xxx
```

**Logic to memorise:** Drawings *reduced* the closing capital, so add them back to reveal the true profit. Fresh capital *inflated* the closing capital, so strip it out.

Capital itself = **Assets − Liabilities**, found by preparing a **statement of affairs** at each date (Lesson 2).

### Worked example — Capital comparison

Wanjiru runs a boutique in Nakuru. Her statement of affairs shows:

- Capital at 1 January 2025: Sh.340,000 (assets 520,000 − liabilities 180,000)
- Capital at 31 December 2025: Sh.560,000 (assets 780,000 − liabilities 220,000)

During the year she withdrew Sh.5,000 per month for household expenses and, in June, injected Sh.100,000 from her savings into the business.

**Required:** Profit for the year ended 31 December 2025.

**Solution:**

```
Capital at 31 December 2025                        560,000
Add: Drawings (5,000 × 12)                          60,000
                                                   620,000
Less: Fresh capital introduced                    (100,000)
                                                   520,000
Less: Capital at 1 January 2025                   (340,000)
Profit for the year                                180,000
```

Check the logic: without drawings or fresh capital, profit would be 560,000 − 340,000 = 220,000. She took out 60,000 (which depressed closing capital) and put in 100,000 (which inflated it): 220,000 + 60,000 − 100,000 = **180,000** ✓.

> **Exam trap:** The two classic errors are (a) *deducting* drawings instead of adding them back, and (b) *adding* fresh capital instead of deducting it. Write the pro-forma above and fill it in — do not improvise the signs.

---

pages.title: 3. Spotting Drawings and Fresh Capital
pages.markdown:
## 3. Spotting Drawings and Fresh Capital

Because the cash book mixes business and personal items, scan it for:

**Drawings (debit the capital account):**

- Rent/electricity/telephone for premises shared with the owner's residence (apportion on a fair basis, e.g. floor area)
- Life insurance premiums of the proprietor paid from business cash
- Household expenses, school fees, personal gifts met from business cash
- Private loans to friends/relatives from business cash
- Goods taken from the business for personal consumption

**Fresh capital introduced (credit the capital account):**

- Cash injected directly by the proprietor/partners
- Matured **life insurance policy** proceeds retained in the business
- Interest/dividends on the proprietor's *private* investments banked into the business
- Income from non-business property put into the business

Unless these are identified and segregated, business income is misstated and the statement of affairs will not articulate.

![Single entry vs double entry](https://jorjhskqykkajcaiweqn.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/course-media/ca11/m09-accounts-from-incomplete-records/illustrations/single-vs-double-entry.png)

pages.title: 4. When Capital Comparison Gives a Loss
pages.markdown:
## 4. When Capital Comparison Gives a Loss

The method works symmetrically for losses — a negative answer is a *loss*, not an error. **Mini-example:** Baraka's capital was Sh.900,000 at 1 January and Sh.750,000 at 31 December. He withdrew Sh.120,000 during the year and introduced no fresh capital.

Profit = 750,000 + 120,000 − 0 − 900,000 = **(30,000)** — a loss of Sh.30,000. The brackets (or the word "loss") must be shown; presenting "profit (30,000)" without labelling it a loss loses the mark. Sanity check: capital fell by 150,000 despite no fresh investment, but 120,000 of that fall is explained by drawings — the remaining 30,000 is the trading loss.

pages.title: 5. Capital Comparison vs Full Final Accounts
pages.markdown:
## 5. Capital Comparison vs Full Final Accounts

The capital comparison method is a **shortcut**, used when revenue and expense detail is unobtainable. Its profit is an *estimate* — it cannot show *how* the profit arose (gross profit, expense breakdown). Where the records permit — cash book plus day books, i.e. quasi single entry — the fuller technique of **Lesson 3** is better: complete the double entry, then prepare a proper trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet.

Think of the two approaches as a ladder:

1. **Pure/simple single entry** → only capital comparison is possible.
2. **Quasi single entry** → complete the records (Lesson 3) → full final accounts; capital comparison remains a useful *check* on the computed profit.

Indeed, a shrewd exam technique: after preparing final accounts from completed records, run a quick capital comparison — if the two profits disagree, an error hides in the adjustments.

A final caution: the capital comparison profit and the *change in the bank balance* are different things. Drawings, fresh capital, loan repayments and asset purchases all move cash without touching profit. Never present "closing bank minus opening bank" as profit — it is the commonest zero-mark answer in this topic.

pages.title: 6. Worked Mini-Example: Mixed Adjustments
pages.markdown:
## 6. Worked Mini-Example: Mixed Adjustments

Otieno's statements of affairs show capital of Sh.200,000 at 1 January and Sh.260,000 at 31 December. During the year: cash drawings 25,000; goods taken for personal use 5,000; a matured life policy of 15,000 retained in the business; cash introduced 25,000.

- Drawings = 25,000 + 5,000 = **30,000** (goods taken are drawings too).
- Fresh capital = 15,000 + 25,000 = **40,000**.
- Profit = 260,000 + 30,000 − 40,000 − 200,000 = **50,000** ✓.

Check the logic: raw growth is 60,000; drawings explain 30,000 of apparent growth that was really withdrawals (add back → 90,000); fresh capital explains 40,000 of growth that was not earned (deduct → 50,000).

Note the goods taken (5,000) are valued at *cost* — drawings in kind are never valued at selling price. Had Otieno taken goods worth 5,000 at cost that would have sold for 8,000, drawings are still 5,000: the business lost cost, not the foregone profit.

pages.title: Key Terms
pages.markdown:
## Key Terms

- **Incomplete records ("single entry")** — partial books kept without full double entry; no true system.
- **Pure / simple / quasi single entry** — personal accounts only; plus cash book; plus subsidiary books (the examined type).
- **Capital comparison (net worth) method** — profit = (closing capital + drawings − fresh capital) − opening capital.
- **Statement of affairs** — assets-and-liabilities statement used to find capital when ledgers are incomplete.

pages.title: Module Summary
pages.markdown:
## Module Summary

- Small businesses often keep incomplete records; "single entry" is not a real system but a label for the resulting gaps.
- Quasi single entry (personal accounts + cash book + day books) is the practical and examined form.
- Profit can be found without a P&L account: compare opening and closing capital, adding back drawings and deducting fresh capital introduced.
- Drawings and fresh capital are often disguised in the cash book — learn the checklists above.

pages.title: Exam Day Tips
pages.markdown:
## Exam Day Tips

1. Always start a capital-comparison answer by computing opening and closing capital (assets − liabilities) — show both.
2. Convert monthly drawings to annual figures (× 12) before adding back.
3. If the question gives a life-insurance maturity retained in the business, treat it as fresh capital, not income.
4. When profit seems implausibly large, recheck the signs: drawings added, fresh capital deducted.
5. State the method's name ("capital comparison / net worth method") — it earns the knowledge mark.

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# The Statement of Affairs

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

1. Prepare a statement of affairs at two dates from incomplete records.
2. Derive opening and closing capital as the balancing figure.
3. Adjust assets for depreciation and deal with part-disposals in the statement of affairs.
4. Compute profit by combining the statement of affairs with the capital comparison method.
5. Distinguish a statement of affairs from a balance sheet on the standard five bases.

---

pages.title: 1. What a Statement of Affairs Is
pages.markdown:
## 1. What a Statement of Affairs Is

A **statement of affairs** lists the assets and liabilities of a business at a given date, in balance-sheet layout, with **capital as the balancing figure** (assets − liabilities). It is prepared from whatever fragments exist:

| Information source | Gives |
|---|---|
| Cash book | Cash balance |
| Bank pass book / statements | Bank balance |
| Personal ledgers | Debtors and creditors |
| Physical count and valuation | Inventory |
| Owner's list of fixed assets less reasonable depreciation | Written-down values of non-current assets |

Because much of it rests on estimates, memory and valuations rather than on a complete double-entry trail, a statement of affairs is **not dependable** in the way a double-entry balance sheet is — but it is the only route to capital when books are incomplete.

### Format

```
                 Statement of affairs as at ............
Liabilities                     Sh.        Assets                     Sh.
Capital (balancing figure)      xxx        Premises                   xxx
Loan, bank overdraft            xxx        Equipment                  xxx
Sundry creditors                xxx        Furniture                  xxx
Bills payable                   xxx        Inventory                  xxx
Outstanding expenses            xxx        Sundry debtors             xxx
                                           Bills receivable           xxx
                                           Cash and bank              xxx
                                           Prepaid expenses           xxx
                                xxx                                   xxx
```

---

pages.title: 2. Comprehensive Worked Example — Kamau Traders
pages.markdown:
## 2. Comprehensive Worked Example — Kamau Traders

Kamau runs a hardware shop in Thika. His records are incomplete. The following information is available:

**At 1 January 2025:** Premises Sh.800,000; equipment Sh.240,000; inventory Sh.150,000; debtors Sh.95,000; bank Sh.60,000; cash Sh.12,000; loan Sh.200,000; creditors Sh.110,000.

**At 31 December 2025:** Inventory Sh.210,000; debtors Sh.130,000; bank Sh.85,000; cash Sh.18,000; loan Sh.150,000; creditors Sh.140,000. Premises and equipment as at 1 January, before depreciation.

**During 2025:** Kamau withdrew Sh.15,000 per month for family expenses. A life insurance policy matured and Sh.120,000 was retained in the business. Depreciate premises at 2.5% and equipment at 10% per annum.

**Required:** (a) Statements of affairs at both dates. (b) Profit for the year.

### Solution (a) — Statements of affairs

```
              Kamau Traders — Statement of affairs
              as at 1 January 2025 and 31 December 2025
Liabilities        1 Jan      31 Dec      Assets             1 Jan      31 Dec
                     Sh.        Sh.                            Sh.        Sh.
Capital (bal.   1,047,000   1,149,000   Premises             800,000   780,000
  figure)                                        (less 2.5% dep.)       (20,000)
Loan              200,000     150,000   Equipment            240,000   216,000
Creditors         110,000     140,000     (less 10% dep.)               (24,000)
                                               Inventory      150,000   210,000
                                               Debtors         95,000   130,000
                                               Bank            60,000    85,000
                                               Cash            12,000    18,000
                1,357,000   1,439,000                         1,357,000 1,439,000
```

Capital workings:

- 1 Jan: assets 1,357,000 − liabilities 310,000 = **1,047,000**
- 31 Dec: assets 1,439,000 − liabilities 290,000 = **1,149,000**

Both sides agree at each date ✓ (1,047,000 + 200,000 + 110,000 = 1,357,000; 1,149,000 + 150,000 + 140,000 = 1,439,000).

### Solution (b) — Profit by capital comparison

```
Capital at 31 December 2025                          1,149,000
Add: Drawings (15,000 × 12)                            180,000
                                                     1,329,000
Less: Fresh capital introduced (insurance maturity)   (120,000)
                                                     1,209,000
Less: Capital at 1 January 2025                     (1,047,000)
Profit for the year                                    162,000
```

> **Exam trap:** Depreciation must be deducted *before* capital is struck — the written-down value goes into the statement of affairs. Students who list premises at 800,000 at both dates overstate closing capital and therefore overstate profit. Also note the insurance maturity is **fresh capital**, not business income.

---

pages.title: 3. Statement of Affairs vs Balance Sheet
pages.markdown:
## 3. Statement of Affairs vs Balance Sheet

A guaranteed 4–6 mark theory question. Learn the five bases:

| Basis | Statement of affairs | Balance sheet |
|---|---|---|
| **Reliability** | Based partly on estimates, assumptions and memory — not fully reliable | Based strictly on double-entry records — verifiable and dependable |
| **Capital** | A **balancing figure** (assets − liabilities) | Derived from the **capital account** in the ledger; both sides must agree |
| **Omission** | Omitted assets/liabilities are hard to detect | Omissions are revealed because the balance sheet will not balance |
| **Valuation** | Arbitrary; no disclosed basis | Scientific — cost less depreciation; changes in basis disclosed |
| **Object** | To **find capital** at two dates (for profit computation) | To show the **financial position** at a date |

![Statement of affairs format](https://jorjhskqykkajcaiweqn.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/course-media/ca11/m09-accounts-from-incomplete-records/illustrations/statement-of-affairs-format.png)

pages.title: 4. Adjusting Fixed Assets: Depreciation and Part-Disposals
pages.markdown:
## 4. Adjusting Fixed Assets: Depreciation and Part-Disposals

Fixed assets enter the statement of affairs at **written-down value** — cost less reasonable accumulated depreciation. Two complications arise:

**Depreciation for the year** must be charged *before* capital is struck (Lesson 2, Kamau: premises 800,000 less 2.5% = 780,000). The rate is given; apply it to cost (or to the given valuation) and deduct.

**Part-disposals during the year:** if an asset was sold, it must not appear in the closing statement at all. Instead:

- Remove the asset's written-down value from the closing list.
- The *proceeds* appear as a cash/bank receipt (and any profit or loss on disposal is captured indirectly through the cash balance in the capital comparison).

**Mini-example:** Equipment stood at Sh.240,000 (1 Jan). During the year equipment with written-down value Sh.40,000 was sold for Sh.45,000 cash; depreciate the remainder at 10%.

- Closing equipment = (240,000 − 40,000) × 90% = **180,000**.
- Bank includes the 45,000 proceeds. The 5,000 profit on disposal is embedded in closing capital — the capital comparison captures it automatically.

pages.title: 5. A Second Mini-Example: Statement of Affairs with Accruals
pages.markdown:
## 5. A Second Mini-Example: Statement of Affairs with Accruals

Incomplete records still contain accruals and prepayments — include them like any balance-sheet item. **Mini-example (one date):** Assets: equipment (WDV) 300,000; inventory 80,000; debtors 60,000; bank 40,000; prepaid rent 12,000. Liabilities: creditors 70,000; outstanding wages 8,000; loan 100,000.

Capital = (300,000 + 80,000 + 60,000 + 40,000 + 12,000) − (70,000 + 8,000 + 100,000) = 492,000 − 178,000 = **314,000**.

Prepayments are assets; outstanding expenses are liabilities — the same definitions as in double entry. Forgetting the 8,000 accrual would overstate capital by 8,000 and overstate profit by the same amount.

pages.title: 6. Errors That Destroy the Capital Figure
pages.markdown:
## 6. Errors That Destroy the Capital Figure

1. **Listing fixed assets at cost** at both dates — depreciation ignored, closing capital overstated, profit overstated.
2. **Including the owner's private assets** (e.g. personal car, residence) in business assets — capital overstated.
3. **Omitting liabilities** the owner "forgot" — especially outstanding expenses and private loans used in the business; capital overstated.
4. **Double-counting drawings** — deducting them in the statement *and* adding them back in the comparison.
5. **Using the bank balance as cash** without reconciling — unpresented cheques distort both statements.

Run this five-point check before computing profit; each error flows straight into the profit figure.

pages.title: 7. Proving Each Statement Balances
pages.markdown:
## 7. Proving Each Statement Balances

Before computing profit, prove each statement of affairs: the total of the liabilities side (including the capital balancing figure) must equal total assets. Kamau's 1 January statement: 1,047,000 + 200,000 + 110,000 = 1,357,000 = assets ✓. This is not busywork — if the two sides disagree, an asset or liability is missing or a depreciation working is wrong, and the capital (hence profit) is wrong. In the exam, write the check as one line; markers award it as a method mark, and it is the fastest way to catch a transposition before it poisons the profit computation.

pages.title: 8. Quick Self-Test
pages.markdown:
## 8. Quick Self-Test

1. A statement of affairs lists assets of 600,000 and liabilities of 220,000. Capital is… *(380,000 — the balancing figure.)*
2. Equipment cost 100,000; the question says "depreciate at 20%". It enters the statement of affairs at… *(80,000 — depreciate first, then strike capital.)*
3. True or false: a statement of affairs can detect an omitted liability because it will not balance. *(False — that is the balance sheet's advantage; in a statement of affairs the omission is absorbed into the capital balancing figure, which is exactly why it is less reliable.)*

If any answer surprised you, re-read sections 1–3 before attempting Lesson 3.

pages.title: Key Terms
pages.markdown:
## Key Terms

- **Statement of affairs** — assets and liabilities statement with capital as the balancing figure, built from incomplete records.
- **Balancing figure** — capital = total assets − total liabilities.
- **Written-down value** — cost less accumulated (reasonable) depreciation, used for fixed assets in the statement.
- **Net worth method** — another name for the capital comparison method.

pages.title: Module Summary
pages.markdown:
## Module Summary

- The statement of affairs reconstructs assets and liabilities at two dates; capital is the plug figure.
- Fixed assets enter at written-down value after charging reasonable depreciation.
- The two capitals feed the capital comparison computation: + drawings, − fresh capital, − opening capital = profit.
- It resembles a balance sheet but differs in reliability, the nature of capital, omission detection, valuation basis and objective.

pages.title: Exam Day Tips
pages.markdown:
## Exam Day Tips

1. Rule two columns (both dates) on one statement — it halves your writing and markers love it.
2. Depreciate first, then strike capital. Show the depreciation working.
3. Prove each statement balances (liabilities side = assets side) before computing profit.
4. In the theory comparison, use the exact five headings: reliability, capital, omission, valuation, object.
5. Never call it a balance sheet — the name "statement of affairs" itself carries a mark.

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# Techniques for Completing Incomplete Records

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

1. Build a cash and bank summary and use its balancing figure to find cash sales or cash purchases.
2. Prepare total debtors and total creditors accounts to find credit sales and credit purchases as balancing figures.
3. Adjust nominal accounts for prepayments, accruals and private (non-business) items.
4. Apply mark-up and margin relationships to derive missing sales, purchases or gross profit figures.
5. Outline the general procedure for converting incomplete records to double entry and extracting a trial balance.

---

pages.title: 1. The General Approach
pages.markdown:
## 1. The General Approach

Rather than estimating profit by capital comparison, the fuller technique is to **complete the double entry first**, then prepare proper final accounts:

1. Open ledger accounts with the **opening balances** of assets, liabilities and capital.
2. Take each book of original entry in turn (cash book, sales day book, purchases day book, returns books, bills books) and post whatever was never posted — nominal and real accounts as well as personal ones.
3. Post discount-column totals to **discounts allowed** and **discounts received**.
4. Sift the cash book for **private items**: the proprietor's personal receipts credited to capital; personal payments debited to capital (drawings); shared expenses (e.g. rent of shared premises) apportioned on a fair basis.
5. Total the debtors' and creditors' schedules; eliminate any revenue/expense items hiding in them; post the totals to total debtors/total creditors accounts.
6. Extract a **trial balance** — it will disclose mistakes made in the adjustments.

Two workhorse techniques supply the missing figures: the **cash/bank summary** and **control (total) accounts**.

---

pages.title: 2. Derivation of Information from the Cash Book
pages.markdown:
## 2. Derivation of Information from the Cash Book

Analyse all cash and bank receipts and payments under significant heads in a **Cash and Bank Summary**. If a figure is missing (often cash sales or cash purchases), it emerges as the **balancing figure**.

### Worked example — Cash and bank summary (adapted from the study text)

Particulars for a firm for 2025 (Sh.):

Cash balance 1 Jan 250; bank overdraft 1 Jan 5,400; cash purchases 3,000; collections from debtors 45,600; sale of old furniture 750; purchase of machinery 12,000; payments to creditors 26,370; expenses 8,450; fresh capital brought in 5,000; drawings 3,230; cash balance 31 Dec 310; bank balance 31 Dec 1,180.

```
                        Cash and Bank Summary
Dr (receipts)                              Sh.      Cr (payments)                 Sh.
Cash balance 1-1-2025                       250      Bank overdraft 1-1-2025     5,400
Collections from debtors                 45,600      Cash purchases              3,000
Sale of old furniture                       750      Purchase of machinery      12,000
Fresh capital brought in                  5,000      Payments to creditors      26,370
Cash sales (balancing figure)             8,340      Expenses                    8,450
                                                   Drawings                    3,230
                                                   Cash balance 31-12-2025       310
                                                   Bank balance 31-12-2025    1,180
                                           59,940                                59,940
```

The debit side is short by **Sh.8,340** — the only plausible source of unrecorded cash inflow is **cash sales**. Post the analysed totals to the ledger; the summary must reconcile to the cash and bank books.

> **Exam trap:** The balancing figure is not automatically "cash sales" — reason it out. If receipts are short, it is an unrecorded *inflow* (cash sales, fresh capital); if payments are short, an unrecorded *outflow* (cash purchases, drawings). Say which, and why, in one line.

---

pages.title: 3. Total Debtors and Total Creditors Accounts
pages.markdown:
## 3. Total Debtors and Total Creditors Accounts

Where only personal ledgers exist, the **total debtors account** finds credit sales and the **total creditors account** finds credit purchases — each as a balancing figure.

### Worked example (continuing the firm above)

Additional information: opening debtors 15,000; closing debtors 25,600; discount allowed 1,870; opening creditors 12,300; closing creditors 13,800; discount received 1,130.

```
                        Sundry Creditors Account
Dr                                              Cr
Cash (paid to creditors)     26,370   Balance b/d (opening)      12,300
Discount received             1,130   Purchases — credit (bal.     29,000
Balance c/d (closing)        13,800     figure)
                             41,300                                41,300
```

Credit purchases = **Sh.29,000**; total purchases = 29,000 + cash purchases 3,000 = **Sh.32,000**.

```
                         Sundry Debtors Account
Dr                                              Cr
Balance b/d (opening)        15,000   Cash (from debtors)        45,600
Sales — credit (bal. figure) 58,070   Discount allowed            1,870
                                      Balance c/d (closing)      25,600
                             73,070                                73,070
```

Credit sales = **Sh.58,070**; total sales = 58,070 + cash sales 8,340 = **Sh.66,410**.

> **Exam trap:** Discounts go on the *opposite* side from cash: discount **received** is a debit in the creditors account; discount **allowed** is a credit in the debtors account. Bills receivable received from debtors are credited to debtors; bills payable issued to creditors are debited to creditors.

---

pages.title: 4. Mark-Up and Margin
pages.markdown:
## 4. Mark-Up and Margin

Where sales or purchases are still missing, the **gross profit relationship** unlocks them:

- **Mark-up** = Gross profit ÷ Cost of sales (profit expressed on cost)
- **Margin** = Gross profit ÷ Sales (profit expressed on selling price)

Conversions (with m = mark-up, g = margin as decimals):

```
Margin  = m ÷ (1 + m)          Mark-up = g ÷ (1 − g)
Cost of sales = Sales ÷ (1 + m) = Sales × (1 − g)
```

### Worked example

Using the firm above: opening stock 20,000; purchases 32,000; closing stock 15,000; sales 66,410.

- Cost of sales = 20,000 + 32,000 − 15,000 = **37,000**
- Gross profit = 66,410 − 37,000 = **29,410**
- Mark-up = 29,410 ÷ 37,000 = **79.5%**; margin = 29,410 ÷ 66,410 = **44.3%**
- Check: 79.5% ÷ 1.795 = 44.3% ✓

**Using the relationship in reverse** (the examined skill): a trader maintains a steady gross margin of 25% on sales and sold goods for Sh.200,000. Then cost of sales = 200,000 × (1 − 0.25) = **Sh.150,000** and gross profit = **Sh.50,000**. If instead the mark-up is given as 25% on cost: cost of sales = 200,000 ÷ 1.25 = **Sh.160,000**, gross profit **Sh.40,000**.

> **Exam trap:** The single most common error is applying a mark-up percentage to *sales* or a margin to *cost*. Read the words: "mark-up **on cost**" divides sales; "margin **on sales**" multiplies sales. When in doubt, test with 25%: mark-up 25% on cost 100 → price 125; margin 25% on price 125 → cost 93.75 — different answers, so the base matters.

---

pages.title: 5. Putting It All Together
pages.markdown:
## 5. Putting It All Together

A typical KASNEB question chains the techniques: cash summary → cash sales; total debtors → credit sales; total creditors → credit purchases; stock account → cost of sales; margin → gross profit check; then the trading and profit and loss account and balance sheet as normal. Practise the chain in that order and each balancing figure becomes the next step's input.

pages.title: 6. Nominal Account Adjustments: Prepayments, Accruals and Private Items
pages.markdown:
## 6. Nominal Account Adjustments: Prepayments, Accruals and Private Items

When completing the records, the nominal (expense/income) accounts need the same adjustments as in full double entry:

- **Accruals:** expenses incurred but unpaid at year-end (e.g. outstanding wages 8,000) are *added* to the cash paid to give the P&L charge, and appear as current liabilities.
- **Prepayments:** expenses paid in advance (e.g. prepaid rent 12,000) are *deducted* from cash paid; the prepayment is a current asset.
- **Private items** in the cash book are stripped out: personal payments → drawings (debit capital); personal receipts banked in → fresh capital (credit capital); shared expenses (rent of shared premises) → apportioned on a fair basis, the private portion to drawings.

**Mini-example:** Cash paid for rent 120,000; prepaid rent at year-end 12,000; one-third of the premises is the owner's residence. Business rent = (120,000 − 12,000) × 2/3 = **72,000**; drawings = 108,000 × 1/3 = **36,000**; prepayment asset = 12,000 × 2/3 = **8,000** (the private third of the prepayment, 4,000, is also drawings).

pages.title: 7. The Trial Balance as Error Check
pages.markdown:
## 7. The Trial Balance as Error Check

After posting all completions, **extract a trial balance**. Its agreement proves the double entry is arithmetically complete — the single most powerful error check in this topic. If it does not agree:

1. Re-check each balancing figure (cash sales, credit sales, credit purchases) — a sign error here unbalances everything downstream.
2. Confirm every private-item adjustment hit *both* sides (drawings ↔ cash; fresh capital ↔ cash).
3. Confirm discounts were posted to the right accounts (discount allowed/received).
4. Only then consider a suspense account — but at CA11, finding the error scores more than opening one.

A trial balance that agrees does not prove every figure is *correct* — errors of principle (e.g. treating drawings as an expense) still balance — so keep the classification rules of Lessons 1–2 in mind throughout.

pages.title: Key Terms
pages.markdown:
## Key Terms

- **Cash and bank summary** — analysed receipts and payments; the balancing figure reveals cash sales/purchases.
- **Total debtors account** — control account yielding credit sales as the balancing figure.
- **Total creditors account** — control account yielding credit purchases as the balancing figure.
- **Mark-up** — gross profit as a percentage of cost of sales. **Margin** — gross profit as a percentage of sales.
- **Balancing figure** — the unknown found by making both sides of an account/summary agree.

pages.title: Module Summary
pages.markdown:
## Module Summary

- Complete the double entry first: post unposted items from each book, sift out private transactions, apportion shared expenses.
- The cash/bank summary's balancing figure identifies missing cash sales or purchases.
- Total debtors/creditors accounts identify missing credit sales/purchases; discounts sit on the opposite side from cash.
- Mark-up (on cost) and margin (on sales) interconvert and derive missing sales, cost of sales or gross profit.

pages.title: Exam Day Tips
pages.markdown:
## Exam Day Tips

1. Draw the T-account and label the balancing figure explicitly ("credit sales (balancing figure)") — the label earns marks.
2. Keep a consistent Sh. column; control accounts must balance to the shilling.
3. Before using a margin, confirm its base (cost or sales) — underline the words in the question.
4. After finding each figure, ask "what does this unlock next?" — chain the techniques forward.
5. Always extract (or at least attempt) a trial balance after completing the entries; agreement is your error check.

chapters.module: Financial Statements of a Not-for-Profit Organisation
chapters.lesson: Not-for-Profit Organisations — Features and the Receipts and Payments Account

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# Not-for-Profit Organisations — Features and the Receipts and Payments Account

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

1. Distinguish a not-for-profit organisation from a profit-making organisation across at least six bases of comparison.
2. State the three financial statements prepared by a not-for-profit organisation and the purpose of each.
3. Define a receipts and payments account and list its characteristics, advantages and the method of preparing it.
4. Prepare a receipts and payments account from a given cash book, with correctly classified headings and a balancing closing balance.
5. Explain the correct accounting treatment of special receipts — subscriptions, donations, grants, legacies, endowment funds, entrance fees, life membership fees, sale of old assets and special purpose funds — distinguishing capital from revenue treatment.

---

pages.title: 1. What is a not-for-profit organisation?
pages.markdown:
## 1. What is a not-for-profit organisation?

A **not-for-profit organisation** (also called a non-trading organisation or non-trading concern) is an entity established **not to earn profits for owners** but to promote art, culture, sports, education, health or some other social cause. Medical institutions, charitable trusts, welfare societies, educational institutions, sports clubs and professional associations are all examples.

A common myth is that not-for-profit organisations never make a profit. In reality they frequently generate surpluses from activities such as bars, restaurants, tournaments or letting out halls — but the **way the profit is handled is different**: it is not distributed to owners as dividends but is reinvested to further the organisation's objectives. Any surplus is transferred to the **capital fund** (the NPO equivalent of capital), not to a capital account for distribution.

### NPO vs profit-making organisation — comparison

| Basis of comparison | Profit organisation | Not-for-profit organisation |
|---|---|---|
| **Meaning** | A legal entity operating to earn profit for the owner | A legal entity operating to serve society as a whole |
| **Motive** | Profit motive | Service motive |
| **Form** | Sole proprietorship, partnership firm or company | Club, trust, public hospital, society, etc. |
| **Management** | Sole proprietor, partners or directors | Trustees, committees or governing bodies |
| **Source of revenue** | Sale of goods and services | Donations, subscriptions, membership fees, etc. |
| **Commenced through** | Capital contributed by the owners | Funds from donations, subscriptions, government grants, etc. |
| **Financial statements** | Income statement, statement of financial position and cash flow statement | Receipts & payments account, income & expenditure account, statement of financial position |
| **Money earned over and above** | Profit transferred to capital account | Surplus transferred to capital fund |

**Exam trap:** KASNEB loves asking why NPOs prepare financial statements at all, since they have no profit motive. Answer: (i) to know whether current incomes are sufficient to meet current expenses; (ii) to know the financial position at the end of each period.

pages.title: 2. The final accounts of a not-for-profit organisation
pages.markdown:
## 2. The final accounts of a not-for-profit organisation

The final accounts comprise three statements:

1. **Receipts and payments account** — a summary of cash transactions for the period (this lesson).
2. **Income and expenditure account** — the NPO equivalent of the profit and loss account; it discloses the **surplus or deficit** for the period (Lesson 2).
3. **Statement of financial position** — shows assets, liabilities and the capital fund at a point in time (Lesson 3).

pages.title: 3. Receipts and payments account — nature and definition
pages.markdown:
## 3. Receipts and payments account — nature and definition

> "A receipts and payments account is a **summarised cash book** (cash and bank) for a given period."

It is simply a summary of the cash transactions as they appear in the cash book, analysed and classified under suitable headings, including the opening and closing balances. With the help of this account, plus additional information (accruals, prepayments, depreciation), an **income and expenditure account** is prepared to disclose the true results. Note this carefully: **a receipts and payments account on its own cannot disclose the true surplus or deficit** of the organisation — it records cash only, with no regard for whether receipts or payments relate to the current period, and it includes capital items.

All the information needed to prepare it comes from the cash book. Its closing balance indicates **cash in hand and cash at bank** at the year end.

### Characteristics

1. It is an abridged summary of the cash book.
2. All cash receipts during the year are recorded on the **left-hand (debit) side**; all cash payments on the **right-hand (credit) side**, in classified form.
3. Cash receipts and payments of **both capital and revenue nature** are recorded here.
4. **Only cash transactions** are recorded — no accruals, no depreciation, no outstanding items.
5. It generally shows a **debit balance**. With a bank overdraft, the net balance may be credit; a nil balance is rare.
6. Its closing balance shows closing cash in hand and cash at bank.
7. **It is NOT an account within the double-entry system — it is a statement only.** You cannot post journal entries to it.
8. It is prepared on the last day of the accounting year.

### Advantages

1. Total receipts and total payments under various heads are available **at a glance**.
2. The cash in hand at the year end can be ascertained.
3. It verifies the cash book: total of the debit side of the cash book agrees with total receipts; total of the credit side agrees with total payments.

### Method of preparation

- Heading: *Receipts and Payments Account for the year ended 31 December 20XX*.
- Left side = "Receipts"; right side = "Payments".
- It **starts** with last year's closing cash in hand and cash at bank (opening balance) and **closes** with the current year's closing cash in hand and cash at bank.

![Receipts and payments vs income and expenditure](https://jorjhskqykkajcaiweqn.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/course-media/ca11/m10-financial-statements-of-a-not-for-profit-organisation/illustrations/receipts-vs-payments-vs-income-expenditure.png)

pages.title: 4. Worked example — preparing the receipts and payments account
pages.markdown:
## 4. Worked example — preparing the receipts and payments account

From the following cash book of the **Jabari Sports Club**, prepare the receipts and payments account for the year ended 31 December 2025.

| Receipts | Sh. | Payments | Sh. |
|---|---|---|---|
| Balance b/d: Cash in hand | 48,000 | Rent | 104,000 |
| Balance b/d: Bank | 120,000 | Salaries | 240,000 |
| Subscriptions | 560,000 | Electricity | 36,000 |
| Hall hire (rent received) | 60,000 | Stationery | 18,000 |
| Donations | 75,000 | Repairs | 22,000 |
| Sale of old newspapers | 12,000 | Purchase of equipment | 85,000 |
| Sale of old equipment | 25,000 | Honorarium | 15,000 |

*(This is the same Jabari Sports Club whose income and expenditure account and statement of financial position we prepare in Lessons 2 and 3 — the figures carry through the whole module.)*

**Solution — Jabari Sports Club, Receipts and Payments Account for the year ended 31 December 2025**

```
                                    Dr                                                        Cr
Receipts                                                         Sh.          Payments                                     Sh.
Balance b/d (1 Jan 2025):
  Cash in hand                                                    48,000       Rent                                         104,000
  Bank                                                           120,000       Salaries                                     240,000
Subscriptions                                                    560,000       Electricity                                   36,000
Hall hire (rent received)                                         60,000       Stationery                                    18,000
Donations                                                         75,000       Repairs                                       22,000
Sale of old newspapers                                            12,000       Purchase of equipment                         85,000
Sale of old equipment                                             25,000       Honorarium                                    15,000
                                                                              Balance c/d (31 Dec 2025):
                                                                                Cash in hand and bank                      380,000
                                                                                ─────────
                                       ─────────                                                           ─────────
                                         900,000                                                           900,000
                                       ═════════                                                           ═════════
Balance b/d (1 Jan 2026)                                         380,000
```

Check the arithmetic:

- Total receipts = 48,000 + 120,000 + 560,000 + 60,000 + 75,000 + 12,000 + 25,000 = **900,000** ✓
- Total payments (excluding balance) = 104,000 + 240,000 + 36,000 + 18,000 + 22,000 + 85,000 + 15,000 = **520,000** ✓
- Balance c/d = 900,000 − 520,000 = **380,000** ✓

**Exam trap:** Do not exclude capital receipts (donations for building, sale of old equipment) or capital payments (purchase of equipment) — the receipts and payments account records **all** cash, capital and revenue alike. And never put accruals, depreciation or outstanding subscriptions here — cash only.

pages.title: 5. Special receipts and their accounting treatment
pages.markdown:
## 5. Special receipts and their accounting treatment

This is the most heavily examined theory in the topic. The central question for every special receipt is: **capital receipt or revenue receipt?**

**Capital receipts** go to the **liability side of the statement of financial position** (added to the relevant fund or capital fund). **Revenue receipts** go to the **credit side of the income and expenditure account**.

### (a) Subscriptions
A **recurring** income and one of the main sources of revenue — credited to the income and expenditure account **after adjusting** for subscriptions in arrears (accrued) and subscriptions received in advance (prepaid), so that only the current year's subscriptions appear. **Exception:** subscriptions received for a specific purpose (e.g. tournament fund, construction of a pavilion) are **capitalised** — shown on the liability side of the statement of financial position.

### (b) Donations
A gift from a person, firm or company:
- **Specific donations** (for a building, library, furniture) → **capital receipts**, liability side; expenditure on that purpose is deducted and the balance shown until used up.
- **General donations** → treatment depends on **amount**: a comparatively **small** amount is treated as **income**; a **big** amount is treated as **capital** (liability side).

### (c) Grants
Grants from central, state or local bodies **for routine expenses** → treated as **income**. Grants for a **specific purpose** (construction of buildings, purchase of X-ray equipment) → **capitalised**.

### (d) Legacy
Amount received under the will of a deceased person → a **capital receipt** (liability side). If the amount is **small** it may be treated as income. In the absence of specific information, **capitalise it**.

### (e) Endowment fund
A fund meant as a **permanent** means of support → **capital receipt**, always.

### (f) Entrance fees
Accountants differ: some say capitalise (it is paid only once per member — non-recurring); others say treat as income (the club receives entrance fees regularly each year as new members join). **In the absence of specific instruction in the question, you may treat it either way — but you must append a note justifying your choice.** (This note earns the mark.)

### (g) Sale of old assets
The amount realised is a **capital receipt** credited to the asset account. But the **profit or loss on sale is revenue** and goes to the income and expenditure account.

### (h) Sale of newspapers and periodicals
Treated as **income** — credited to the income and expenditure account.

### (i) Expenditure stock items
Items like stationery and sports materials (bats, balls): the **unused closing stock is deducted** from total spent, so only the amount actually used up is debited to the income and expenditure account:

pages.title: 5. Special receipts and their accounting treatment (continued)
pages.markdown:
## 5. Special receipts and their accounting treatment (continued)

```
Stock of stationery (opening)            xxx
Add: purchases during the year           xxx
                                         xxx
Less: stock of stationery (closing)     (xxx)   → asset in statement of financial position
Stationery used during the year          xxx    → debited to income and expenditure account
```

### (j) Sale of scraps, grass, etc.
**Revenue receipts** — shown on the income side.

### (k) Life membership fees
A lump sum paid in lieu of annual subscriptions for life. Since service must be rendered for a long time without further payment → **capital receipt, capitalised**.

### (l) Payment of honorarium
Amount paid for a specific service rendered (singers, dancers) → shown on the **expenditure side** of the income and expenditure account.

### (m) Special purpose funds
Where a fund exists for a specific purpose (tournament fund, charity fund, prize fund, endowment fund), **do not** show its income and expenses in the income and expenditure account. Instead, **add income to the fund and deduct expenses from the fund** on the liability side of the statement of financial position.

![Capital vs revenue treatment of special receipts](https://jorjhskqykkajcaiweqn.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/course-media/ca11/m10-financial-statements-of-a-not-for-profit-organisation/illustrations/special-receipts-treatment.png)

pages.title: Key terms
pages.markdown:
## Key terms

- **Not-for-profit organisation** — an entity established to promote a social cause rather than to earn profit for owners; surpluses are reinvested, not distributed.
- **Capital fund** — the NPO equivalent of capital; accumulated fund to which surpluses are added.
- **Receipts and payments account** — a summarised cash book for the period; a statement, not part of double entry; records all cash receipts and payments, capital and revenue.
- **Capital receipt** — a non-recurring receipt (donations for specific purposes, legacies, life membership) shown on the liability side of the statement of financial position.
- **Revenue receipt** — a recurring receipt (subscriptions, general small donations, sale of newspapers) credited to the income and expenditure account.
- **Specific donation/grant** — a donation or grant earmarked for a particular purpose; capitalised.
- **Legacy** — amount received under a deceased person's will; capitalised unless the amount is small.
- **Endowment fund** — a fund providing permanent means of support; a capital receipt.
- **Entrance fees** — fee on admission of members; capital or revenue — state your assumption with a justifying note.
- **Special purpose fund** — a fund for a defined purpose (tournament, prize, charity); its income and expenses bypass the income and expenditure account and adjust the fund directly.

pages.title: Module summary (so far)
pages.markdown:
## Module summary (so far)

- NPOs serve society; profit organisations serve owners — this drives different statements and different treatment of surpluses.
- The receipts and payments account is a **cash-only summary statement** (not double entry) covering capital and revenue cash flows, opening with last year's closing cash and closing with this year's.
- Special receipts must be classified as **capital** (statement of financial position, liability side) or **revenue** (income and expenditure account): specific donations, grants for specific purposes, legacies, endowment funds and life membership fees are capital; ordinary subscriptions, small general donations and sale of newspapers are revenue; entrance fees are either, with a justifying note.

pages.title: Exam day tips
pages.markdown:
## Exam day tips

1. When asked to distinguish NPOs from profit organisations, give the comparison in **table form** — markers award per valid basis.
2. Never put non-cash items (depreciation, accruals, outstanding subscriptions) in the receipts and payments account — it is **cash only**.
3. "State with reasons" the treatment of a special receipt: always link the reason to **capital vs revenue** and where it appears.
4. For entrance fees, the note justifying your choice is what earns the mark — never leave it out.
5. If the question is silent on a legacy's size, **capitalise it** — that is the book's default rule.

chapters.module: Financial Statements of a Not-for-Profit Organisation

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# The Income and Expenditure Account

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

1. Define the income and expenditure account and explain the matching principle as applied to it.
2. Prepare a subscription account (T-account) incorporating arrears, advances, bad debts written off and cash received.
3. Convert receipts and payments information into accrual-based income and expenditure using adjustments for outstanding items, prepayments, stock of consumables, depreciation and profit/loss on disposal.
4. Prepare an income and expenditure account that balances to the correct surplus or deficit.
5. Treat special items correctly: prizes in hand, bar/restaurant trading profits, leave allowances and bonuses, and special purpose fund income/expenses.

---

pages.title: 1. Nature of the income and expenditure account
pages.markdown:
## 1. Nature of the income and expenditure account

The **income and expenditure account** is a **revenue (nominal) account** prepared by a non-profit organisation to ascertain the **surplus or deficit** for a particular period. Only **revenue receipts and revenue expenses** are recorded: all revenue expenses of the current year on the **debit side**, all revenue incomes of the current year on the **credit side**. The difference is the surplus (credit balance) or deficit (debit balance), which is transferred to the **capital fund** in the statement of financial position.

The comparison of the two sides shows whether current expenses are being met out of current income. The principles are exactly the same as for a trading and profit and loss account — above all, the **matching principle**:

- (a) **No item of capital nature** is included — but **all revenue items** are entered.
- (b) Income and expenses must **relate only to the year concerned** — items relating to past or future years are excluded.
- (c) The **whole** of the income or expense for the year is included, **even if some amounts are outstanding** (accrued) or paid in advance.

So preparing this account is essentially a conversion exercise: take the cash figures from the receipts and payments account and **adjust them for accruals and prepayments**.

pages.title: 2. The subscription account — the examiner's favourite working
pages.markdown:
## 2. The subscription account — the examiner's favourite working

Subscriptions are the main income of most clubs, and the computation is almost always tested. Build the T-account like this (using our worked data):

**Jabari Sports Club — data for year ended 31 December 2025**

- Subscriptions received in cash during the year: **Sh.560,000**
- Of this, Sh.40,000 related to 2024 and Sh.55,000 related to 2026 (received in advance)
- Subscriptions in arrears at 31 December 2025 (still unpaid): **Sh.35,000**

```
                              Subscription Account
                        Sh.                                   Sh.
Balance b/d (arrears, 1 Jan)      40,000   Cash (received)              560,000
Income and expenditure           500,000   Balance c/d (arrears, 31 Dec) 35,000
Balance c/d (advance, 31 Dec)     55,000
                                 ───────                            ───────
                                 595,000                            595,000
                                 ═══════                            ═══════
Balance b/d (1 Jan 2026):
  Arrears                          35,000
  Advance                          55,000
```

Derivation: subscriptions for 2025 = 560,000 − 40,000 (past year) − 55,000 (next year, advance) + 35,000 (current year, accrued) = **Sh.500,000** ✓. Both sides total 595,000 and balance.

**Logic to memorise:** Debit side — opening arrears (owed to us at start) + income for the year + closing advance (we owe the members service). Credit side — cash received + closing arrears (still owed to us). The balancing figure is the income and expenditure transfer.

**Exam traps:**

- If 10% of opening arrears were never received and written off (as in the book's Jenga Afya question), debit the income and expenditure account with the **bad debt written off** and credit the subscription account.
- Subscriptions received **for a specific purpose** (tournament fund, pavilion) never enter this account — they are capitalised to the fund.

pages.title: 3. Converting other cash figures to accrual figures
pages.markdown:
## 3. Converting other cash figures to accrual figures

The same "opening balance + cash ± closing balance" logic applies to every expense and income line. For each item, draw the small T-account:

**Salaries account (example):** salaries paid Sh.240,000; Sh.20,000 of this was owed at 1 January 2025; Sh.30,000 outstanding at 31 December 2025; plus the secretary's **leave allowance of 5% of basic salary** — a classic book adjustment.

```
                              Salaries Account
                        Sh.                                   Sh.
Cash (paid)                       240,000   Balance b/d (owed 1 Jan)       20,000
Balance c/d (owed 31 Dec)          30,000   Income and expenditure       250,000
                                 ───────                            ───────
                                 270,000                            270,000
```

Charge to income and expenditure = 240,000 − 20,000 + 30,000 = **Sh.250,000** ✓. (In the book's Mbedodo illustration, the leave allowance of 5% × 18,000,000 = 900,000 was added as a separate outstanding expense line — same idea.)

**Rent account (example):** rent paid Sh.104,000; Sh.8,000 of this covers January 2026 (prepaid):

```
Cash 104,000 = Income and expenditure 96,000 + Balance c/d (prepaid) 8,000
```

Charge = 104,000 − 8,000 = **Sh.96,000** ✓.

**Electricity account (example):** paid Sh.36,000; outstanding at year end Sh.6,000:

Charge = 36,000 + 6,000 = **Sh.42,000** ✓.

**Stationery (expenditure stock item):** purchased Sh.18,000; opening stock Sh.4,000; closing stock Sh.5,000:

Used = 4,000 + 18,000 − 5,000 = **Sh.17,000** debited to income and expenditure; closing stock Sh.5,000 is a current asset in the statement of financial position.

**Depreciation** on buildings and equipment and the **loss on sale of old equipment** (proceeds Sh.25,000 vs net book value Sh.30,000 → loss Sh.5,000) are debited to the income and expenditure account. Remember: the **cash proceeds** were a capital receipt in the receipts and payments account, but the **loss** is revenue.

**Bar/restaurant trading profit:** where a club runs a bar or restaurant, prepare a small **trading account** first and transfer only the **profit** to the income and expenditure account (as in the book's Mbedodo bar trading profit of Sh.10,000,000 and Jenga Afya restaurant profit of Sh.1,211,000). Staff consumption of restaurant goods (Jenga Afya: Sh.75,000) is added to purchases as well as treated as staff cost — in the book's solution it was deducted from the accumulated fund as drawings; follow the question's instruction.

**Prizes in hand** (competition prizes not yet awarded) are treated like stock: opening prizes + purchases − prizes awarded = closing prizes in hand (an asset); the prizes awarded are the expense. In the Mbedodo illustration: opening 4,800,000 + competition prizes paid 14,400,000 − closing 2,400,000 = prizes given expense 16,800,000... (the book's own workings are inconsistent here, so in your exam always do the clean stock computation: expense = opening + purchases − closing.)

pages.title: 3. Converting other cash figures to accrual figures (continued)
pages.markdown:
## 3. Converting other cash figures to accrual figures (continued)

**Special purpose fund items** (tournament, prize, charity funds) never touch this account — income is added to the fund and expenses deducted from it on the liability side.

pages.title: 4. Fully worked income and expenditure account
pages.markdown:
## 4. Fully worked income and expenditure account

**Jabari Sports Club — additional information for the year ended 31 December 2025:**

- Subscriptions: cash received Sh.560,000 (includes Sh.40,000 for 2024 and Sh.55,000 for 2026); arrears at 31 Dec 2025: Sh.35,000.
- Hall hire (rent received): Sh.60,000; donations (general, small): Sh.75,000; sale of old newspapers: Sh.12,000.
- Old equipment sold for Sh.25,000 (net book value Sh.30,000).
- Rent paid Sh.104,000 (includes Sh.8,000 for January 2026).
- Salaries paid Sh.240,000 (includes Sh.20,000 owed at 1 Jan 2025); salaries outstanding at 31 Dec 2025: Sh.30,000.
- Electricity paid Sh.36,000; outstanding at year end Sh.6,000.
- Stationery purchased Sh.18,000; opening stock Sh.4,000; closing stock Sh.5,000.
- Repairs Sh.22,000; honorarium Sh.15,000.
- Depreciation: buildings Sh.30,000; equipment Sh.20,000.

**Solution — Jabari Sports Club, Income and Expenditure Account for the year ended 31 December 2025**

```
Incomes                                                     Sh.          Sh.
Subscriptions (W1)                                                     500,000
Hall hire (rent received)                                               60,000
Donations (general)                                                     75,000
Sale of old newspapers                                                  12,000
                                                                       647,000
Expenses
Rent (104,000 − 8,000 prepaid)                              96,000
Salaries (240,000 − 20,000 + 30,000)                      250,000
Electricity (36,000 + 6,000)                               42,000
Stationery used (4,000 + 18,000 − 5,000)                    17,000
Repairs                                                    22,000
Honorarium                                                 15,000
Depreciation: buildings                                    30,000
Depreciation: equipment                                    20,000
Loss on sale of equipment (30,000 − 25,000)                 5,000
Total expenses                                                        (497,000)
Surplus for the year                                                   150,000
```

Verification: total income 500,000 + 60,000 + 75,000 + 12,000 = **647,000** ✓. Total expenses: 96,000 + 250,000 + 42,000 + 17,000 + 22,000 + 15,000 + 30,000 + 20,000 + 5,000 = **497,000** ✓. Surplus = 647,000 − 497,000 = **150,000** ✓.

**W1 — Subscription computation:** 560,000 − 40,000 − 55,000 + 35,000 = 500,000 (see T-account in section 2).

**Exam trap:** the purchase of equipment (Sh.85,000) and the cash proceeds of the equipment sale (Sh.25,000) do **not** appear here — they are capital items. Only the **loss on sale** (Sh.5,000) appears, as an expense.

pages.title: 5. Income and expenditure account vs receipts and payments account
pages.markdown:
## 5. Income and expenditure account vs receipts and payments account

KASNEB frequently asks for the distinction — learn it as a pair:

| Receipts and payments account | Income and expenditure account |
|---|---|
| Summary of **cash** transactions | Accrual-based revenue account |
| Records capital **and** revenue cash flows | Records **revenue items only** |
| **Not** part of double entry — a statement | A **nominal account** within double entry |
| Ignores period to which items relate | Applies the **matching principle** (current year only) |
| Shows cash/bank balance; cannot show surplus | Shows **surplus or deficit** for the period |
| Includes opening and closing cash balances | No opening/closing cash balances |

pages.title: Key terms
pages.markdown:
## Key terms

- **Income and expenditure account** — the NPO's revenue account (nominal account) showing surplus or deficit; revenue items only, on an accruals basis.
- **Surplus / deficit** — excess of income over expenditure (or vice versa); transferred to the capital fund, not distributed.
- **Matching principle** — recognise income and expenses in the period to which they relate, including outstanding and prepaid amounts.
- **Subscriptions in arrears** — amounts owed by members at the year end; a current asset (accrued income).
- **Subscriptions in advance** — amounts received for the next period; a current liability (deferred income).
- **Expenditure stock items** — consumables (stationery, sports materials); only the amount used is expensed, the unused balance is a current asset.
- **Prizes in hand** — competition prizes purchased but not yet awarded; treated like stock.
- **Trading profit (bar/restaurant)** — computed in a separate trading account; only the net profit is transferred to the income and expenditure account.

pages.title: Module summary (so far)
pages.markdown:
## Module summary (so far)

- The income and expenditure account is the NPO equivalent of the profit and loss account: **revenue items only, accruals basis**, with the surplus/deficit transferred to the capital fund.
- Master the **subscription T-account** (opening arrears + income + closing advance = cash + closing arrears) — it is the single most examined working in this topic.
- Every cash figure converts to an accrual figure via: *expense/income = cash paid/received − opening balance + closing balance*, with stock items adjusted for opening and closing stocks.
- Capital items (asset purchases, sale proceeds, specific-purpose receipts) never enter this account — only revenue consequences (depreciation, profit/loss on disposal) do.

pages.title: Exam day tips
pages.markdown:
## Exam day tips

1. Always do the **subscription working first** — it is usually worth 3–4 marks on its own and its figure flows into the main account.
2. Draw a mini T-account for every adjusted item (rent, salaries, electricity); it prevents the classic sign error of adding a prepayment instead of deducting it.
3. Show **workings labelled W1, W2…** — KASNEB awards method marks even if the final figure slips.
4. Double-check that no capital receipt or payment has crept into the account — scan each line and ask "revenue or capital?".
5. A bar or restaurant means a **separate trading account first**; transfer only the profit across.

chapters.lesson: Statement of Financial Position of a Not-for-Profit Organisation

pages.title: Learning objectives
pages.markdown:
# Statement of Financial Position of a Not-for-Profit Organisation

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

1. Describe the layout of a not-for-profit organisation's statement of financial position and explain the capital fund.
2. Compute the opening capital (accumulated) fund from a statement of affairs when it is not given.
3. Correctly place special items — capital receipts, special purpose funds, subscriptions in arrears/advance, outstanding and prepaid expenses, consumable stocks, prizes in hand — in the statement of financial position.
4. Prepare a complete statement of financial position that balances, incorporating the surplus or deficit from the income and expenditure account.
5. Account for the disposal of non-current assets (cost, accumulated depreciation, proceeds, profit/loss) within the NPO framework.

---

pages.title: 1. Layout and the capital fund
pages.markdown:
## 1. Layout and the capital fund

The statement of financial position of an NPO contains **assets and liabilities** in the same way as a profit-making entity, but there is no share capital and no retained earnings. Instead:

- **Assets side:** non-current assets (at cost less accumulated depreciation), outstanding incomes (subscriptions in arrears, accrued interest), prepaid expenses, consumable stocks, prizes in hand, cash in hand and at bank.
- **Liabilities side:** the **capital fund** (accumulated fund), special purpose funds and capital receipts not yet utilised, outstanding expenses, incomes received in advance (subscriptions in advance).
- The **surplus** for the year is **added to the capital fund** (a deficit is deducted).

Think of the capital fund as the NPO's "equity": it represents the net assets accumulated over the organisation's life, built up from entrance fees capitalised, life membership fees, legacies, specific donations and the accumulated surpluses of past years.

pages.title: 2. Computing the opening capital fund — the statement of affairs
pages.markdown:
## 2. Computing the opening capital fund — the statement of affairs

Exam questions often do not give the opening capital fund. You must compute it with a **statement of affairs** (assets minus liabilities at the opening date):

**Jabari Sports Club — statement of affairs as at 1 January 2025**

| | Sh. | Sh. |
|---|---|---|
| **Assets** | | |
| Buildings at cost | 1,500,000 | |
| Equipment at cost | 200,000 | |
| Less: accumulated depreciation — equipment | (60,000) | |
| Stationery stock | 4,000 | |
| Subscriptions in arrears | 40,000 | |
| Cash in hand and at bank | 168,000 | |
| Total assets | | 1,852,000 |
| **Liabilities** | | |
| Salaries outstanding | | (20,000) |
| **Capital fund (accumulated fund) at 1 Jan 2025 (balancing figure)** | | **1,832,000** |

Check: 1,500,000 + 200,000 − 60,000 + 4,000 + 40,000 + 168,000 = **1,852,000**; less 20,000 = **1,832,000** ✓. The two sides balance by construction.

**Exam trap:** every asset and liability must be included at the opening date — especially subscriptions in arrears (asset), subscriptions in advance (liability), outstanding expenses (liability), prepayments (asset) and consumable stocks (asset). Missing one unbalances everything downstream.

pages.title: 3. Where special items go in the statement of financial position
pages.markdown:
## 3. Where special items go in the statement of financial position

| Item | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Specific donations / grants for a purpose | Liability side, as a **fund**; expenditure on the purpose is **deducted from the fund**, balance carried forward until used up |
| General donations (large), legacies, endowment fund, life membership fees | Added to **capital fund** (or shown as separate capital receipts under liabilities) |
| Special purpose funds (tournament, prize, charity) | Liability side; fund income **added**, fund expenses **deducted** — never through the income and expenditure account |
| Subscriptions in arrears | **Current asset** (accrued income) |
| Subscriptions in advance | **Current liability** (deferred income) |
| Outstanding expenses (salaries, electricity) | **Current liabilities** |
| Prepaid expenses (rent paid in advance) | **Current assets** |
| Stationery / consumable stocks, prizes in hand | **Current assets** |
| Surplus for the year | **Added to** the capital fund (deficit deducted) |
| Interest receivable (e.g. on SACCO deposits) | **Current asset** |

pages.title: 4. Non-current asset movements — the disposal working
pages.markdown:
## 4. Non-current asset movements — the disposal working

Continuing the Jabari example, during 2025 the club:

- Purchased new equipment for **Sh.85,000** cash.
- Sold old equipment for **Sh.25,000**; the equipment sold had cost **Sh.50,000** with accumulated depreciation of **Sh.20,000** (net book value Sh.30,000 → **loss on sale Sh.5,000**, already charged in Lesson 2).
- Depreciation for the year: buildings Sh.30,000; equipment Sh.20,000.

```
                                Equipment Account
                        Sh.                                   Sh.
Balance b/d (cost)             200,000   Disposal (cost)               50,000
Cash (additions)                85,000   Balance c/d (cost)           235,000
                                 ───────                            ───────
                                 285,000                            285,000

                   Accumulated Depreciation — Equipment
                        Sh.                                   Sh.
Disposal (dep'n on sold)         20,000   Balance b/d                 60,000
Balance c/d                      60,000   Depreciation for the year   20,000
                                 ───────                            ───────
                                  80,000                             80,000
                                 ═══════                            ═══════
```
